decks.title: How To Win Worlds (170th At Worlds 2026)
decks.author: rongydoge
decks.identity_zh: 勒内·“野狼”·阿斯蒙特: 派对野兽
decks.description_html:
I’ve spent the past ~3 years thinking about how to win worlds.

I think there are 3 main things that have to happen in order to win. Probably there’s some mathematical breakpoint where if you sum your score across all three things and beat that number you’ll win, but since this is all vibes anyway that’s irrelevant. You can overindex on one and underindex on another – the main point is to try to max out each one.

There is a part of you that is unable to lie. Practice listening to that part of yourself. It will tell you how well you’re doing and how well you will do in each category.

1. Prep

You have to know your decks like the back of your hand. That means knowing every card in every slot, it means knowing what your deck can do and can’t do, it means knowing how your deck wins and how your deck loses.

It means knowing every common matchup in the meta on both sides and knowing them cold. Know how each matchup feels early, mid, and late game. Know in each what your opponents can do to surprise you, what you can do to surprise them, and overall how favored or unfavored you are.

The feeling you are going for is feeling on top of the meta. Try to feel totally comfortable into every common matchup. Try to feel like you know the full win-space that corps and runners have access to (regardless of whether each idea or wincon is expressed in a commonly played deck). This doesn’t mean you won’t get surprised on the day by some new brew, but it does mean you know everything you can reasonably expect and that you feel comfortable into all of it.

Listen to the part of yourself that can’t lie. If you feel panicked or underprepared, explore the feeling and be honest with yourself about where the panic is coming from. Then practice intentionally to resolve that panic.

You’ll know if you’ve accomplished this step when you feel no panic about the decks you’re playing or what you might play into. You will feel totally calm, totally prepared, and totally collected.

2. Surf

Worlds is a long tournament that takes extended focus the entire time. In order to win you have to play at the highest level for ~20+ games. It’s extremely difficult to sustain that level of concentration and performance.

Here are some of the best ways I’ve found to do that:

A) Feel prepared going in

Did you do step 1?

B) Narrow your attention

Focus all of your attention on only the game in front of you.

When you sit down and see your opponent’s ID fall back on your meta knowledge. Tap into the part of you that feels calm and comfortable in that matchup. Walk yourself through what you know to be true and how you expect the game to go.

Do not think about any future game while you’re playing. Do not think about what score you need to make day 2/make the cut. Do not think about how many more losses you can “afford”.

Focus all your attention on your opponent and on the game you are playing.

C) Let go

If you lose a round, process it and let it go as quickly as possible. Regardless of the reason – heartbreaking RNG luck, unexpected lines, bad decisions – you need to let it go.

Carrying any negativity from a previous round into the next one is a death sentence. There is no negative emotion that will serve you if you hold onto it at worlds. It will wreck your vision, concentration, and tournament – no matter how painful it is you have to process it and let it go.

If you win a round, process it and let it go as quickly as possible. Unless you learned something that will serve you in your current game, dwelling on your last game will unfocus your attention on the one you’re currently playing.

The ultimate goal is to smooth out your emotional state. Feeling highs and lows during a tournament is normal. Your break between rounds is your time to process and return yourself to your base state of calm, collected, focused, and comfortable.

Listen to the part of yourself that can’t lie. If you’re carrying something from a previous round into your next one, it will tell you. Do what you need to do to let it go before the next game starts.

3. Catch Breaks

Netrunner has chance baked into it. Chance is what obfuscates player skill and makes the game compelling to compete in at the highest level. Without it, the same player would win every game.

You have the least amount of control over this aspect of your tournament. You can’t control your luck, but my experience is that you can influence it through your attitude.

A positive, calm, comfortable attitude can attract luck and good outcomes. A negative attitude combined with a negative outlook and negative thinking can attract bad luck and bad outcomes.

If you’re following step 2 and surfing well that means you will be playing at the top of your game and playing to your outs. This can look like luck from the outside- keeping your mental positive will help you to catch breaks.

I think the part of you that can’t lie is the part that can influence your luck. If that part is telling you today is not your day, you’ve been getting unlucky, you’re fighting a losing battle – you will be. If that part of you isn’t thinking about luck at all – if that part of you is calm, collected, and comfortable about how you’re playing – you’re in the right spot.

The last thing I want to cover is:

4. What To Do When You Know You’re Not Going To Win

Sometimes you find out you’re not going to win worlds while you’re playing in worlds.

This is painful in proportion to how close you felt you got to winning and how much you staked with yourself on accomplishing that goal.

When this happens, be generous to yourself. Try to give yourself what you need in the moment. Sometimes that’s being alone, sometimes that’s being with other people. Listen to the part of yourself that can’t lie.

Sometimes you know you’re not going to win before you even play.

A powerful part of this preparation is that you will always know whether you are on track to win worlds or not. The part of you that always tells the truth will know.

If you still feel panic during step 1 – that’s your truth letting you know you’re not prepared to where you need to be.

If you feel panicked/unprepared/uncollected during the tournament – that’s your truth letting you know you’re not surfing.

If you feel like you’re constantly seeing bad omens – like you’re locked into a negative track that will end in failure – that is your truth telling you that you messed up in step 1 or step 2.

As worlds approached this year the part of me that can’t lie knew I wasn’t going to win. I spent ~3 months wrestling with that knowledge, and my worlds prep was colored by fighting the part of myself that can’t lie.

I tried blaming other people for knowing that I wasn’t going to win. I blamed my friends for the meta and for the cards that got banned. I blamed them for the ways that the game changed and made me uncomfortable in the meta.

The truth is much simpler – I felt resentment about which cards were banned and let that resentment stop me from playing for 9 months. By the time I decided to go, I was 9 months behind in meta-sense and game-sense, and couldn’t catch up in time for worlds.

If, like me, the part of yourself that can’t lie believes you’re not going to win, my advice is to do two things:

1.Try as hard as you can

When you try as hard as you can, you learn things that help you in the future. You learn more about how your body deals with worlds. You learn more about what competing at that level means. You allow yourself to see the gap between your best this year and what would be required to win, which gives you the map to get where you need to go.

2. Be generous to others

The most effective way I’ve found to process the pain of losing is by helping others. It obliterates the self-oriented pain in a kind of incredible way.

Acts of service will help you remember why you’re at worlds in the first place. I didn’t win, but I supported friends as they competed and cheered on my friend when he won – that is an incredible consolation prize.

This was my eighth worlds. I’ve participated every year since 2018 except for 2022. This year was the most fun I’ve ever had at worlds and it’s not particularly close.

See y’all next year.

decks.title: KhusYUM [11th, 12th at Worlds 2026, Undefeated 7-0]
decks.author: London
decks.identity_zh: 玛格达琳·凯诺-切穆泰: 幕后建筑师
decks.description_html:
This is my favorite deck I've built, which is saying a lot considering I'm a perennial corp enjoyer. What can I say, when it's working the deck sings. I would not change a single slot (except maybe 2nd spec to 2nd kk if the meta slows down at all).

It's called KhusYUM because:

  • I reject the common notion that Khusyuk is bad.
  • The spice in this cook tastes great.
  • We love gobbling up agendas while dodging traps and everything else. Yum yum.

The Journey

As my first worlds / large event, I wanted to do some real prep for it. A month ago I put the decklist shell together based on Whiteblade's combo mag, but swapped the dive package for burner khusyuk. I shared a screenshot with The Board of winning a jnet game on 3 accessess, shaper perfection. Eventually AnOddRadish and BBlum picked it up and helped refine the last ~5 slots, including physarum -> botulus, environmental testing -> daily casts, and 3rd specwork -> knickknack (Spiderbro also suggested this). After AnOddRadish suggested joy ride, I added it for Crown of Servers (where I played a sauceless version with a dive package instead of khusyuk, burner, botulus) and found it surprisingly good. Great even.

Including some literal last day converts (I tested with a collaboration between The Board and Meeting of the Minds, dubbed The Motherboard), there were 6 of us who brought the deck, collectively going 25-13 and securing places 11th, 12th, 26th, and 30th (With PeterM / Foilflaws joining me in the top cut and BBlum and Minstrel making day 2). Personally, I did not lose a single game on it, going 7-0. It was so amazing to see the deck deliver across multiple (very good) players, especially given how few reps most of us had on it. On the other hand, it's very reminiscent of prepaid Kate, so in a sense they had been practicing the list for over a decade.

The Meta

Before I get into the deck itself, like any good shaper deck you need to first look at the corp meta. It's pretty fast, see PD, R+, Nuvem. These decks require fast interaction, and R+ plays mostly from hand so big Mag's remote busting engine alone will not cut it. There's also AUco and Ob which can snowball the game if uncontested. Critically, all these corps rely on key pieces that sit in HQ. Fully op, flood, top down, moon pool, superconducting, seamless, measured. Clearly the runner will need to interact quickly and with HQ.

These reasons pushed me away from twinning, especially in anarch. It is too slow for Kingmaking R+ and doesn't access enough. Maybe reg crim could work with better multi access but right now the faction isn't for me. Seb is also fine but I've been off my seb game for a while. Shaper, however, I never doubted. But big mags was never going to be it.

Understanding The Deck

I've been trying to make Whiteblade's madani dzmz engine work for months. With literally one test game the night before, I brought a version with 2 transfers to NANPC Pittsburgh; it was whatever. Transfer open HQ is fun but it doesn't win the game. Back to the drawing board. While I love the madani half of the deck, I don't like the dive combo half. It's too all-in for me. You go to 3 handsize, you don't have clicks to clear tags or police the board, you gotta be ~fully set up. I just want to play control shaper and weave maker's eyes into my turns. Alas, rotato, and cataloguer and conduit ain't it.

Realization. You already want to set up madani dz dz breaker. Add anything else, e.g. muse coal, and khusyuk is fully charged. But that card sucks right? It sees less than a dive and can't steal two. Counterpoint, doing so on a single click is extremely, massively powerful. It is flexible, repeatable (they shuffle!!!), and is not telegraphed. You can win the game out of nowhere this way, but it is also more than a simple gimmick. It is pressure on the corp, telling them hurry the F up or I will end you. No time to play footsies with "is it isn't it an agenda in the remote". And since we are control shaper, forcing them to jam prematurely is another great way to find agendas.

But wait, you say, the math says something like 1/4 to 1/3 of khusyuks whiff. What if I see 18 off R&D and don't win? First of all, makers eye, dive, etc., ... they can all whiff. But yes, you can't expect 7 points on R&D (although the corp should absolutely fear it). That's where the next pressure card comes in: burner. Burner, burner, burner, what can I say about this beautiful card. To anyone who sees an inferior legwork, you are reading the card so, so wrong.

This card provides a truly unique power in the standard cardpool. You get to send the corp's best cards, their bread and butter and wincons, to the least accessible zone short of rfg. We have likened burner to thoughtsieze from MTG. It's less consistent but hits two pieces (!!!), and interacts with "card hit points" in a way that doesn't translate to other games. Removing two cards makes the rest of HQ more vulnerable to accesses, and lucky that, shaper has a repeatable legwork on demand in cupellation. Against the classic 5 card hand, burner into cup sweeps the whole hand, giving shaper S tier HQ pressure. And again, it is often not telegraphed when you may be interested or capable in doing this.

I want to come back to the disruption point as it cannot be overstated. As I outlined in the corp overview, basically all corps rely on pivotal cards they hold in HQ to make plays. Everything else in this category, e.g. phat or holoman, goes on the table and can be pinholed (and put in cup jail if needed). Burner completes the control shaper package by negating corp threats before they can be deployed. Topdown on the bottom? It might be 3 turns to find the spare. Seamless gone? Have fun advancing that basalt and passing turn like a chump so I can steal it. No measured? Oops I guess the runner cheats death yet again. There were so many practice games where it felt like the corp should have won three turns ago before we reflected on how burner removed the corp's key piece(s). When half your deck is about seeing 18 off R&D and sweeping HQ, buying turns this way is a key part of your gameplan. I truly think burner is Shaper's 2nd best card, right behind simulchip.

Playing The Deck

This is a control shaper deck, but it is not big mags. You are not a siege engine breaking down the remote turn after turn. This deck primarily plans to make a few good, high impact runs. It can apply this pressure on all three major servers, so the trick is figuring out when and where to attack.

Usually, the early game involves a degree of setup, depending on the matchup easily 2-4 turns of shaper solitaire or close to it. In most matchups if you get open HQ you can send an early burner, sometimes they don't do a ton, other times they define the game starting turn 1 as the corp fumbles without X piece or you steal a basalt, etc. Mulligan priorities are typically draw > dz > creative/casts/fermenter (depends on matchup and hand) > madani, but really any combination of the above cards will often lead to a keep.

There are some important play patterns to learn regarding the mag installs. Prioritize hardware installs early because you want to setup dz dz madani and because programs can get installed for "free" with madani. In the midgame if you have an unused dz, program installs are fine. If you have dz and madani and want to mag install one this turn and the other next turn along with a madani dump, do madani first. This is because next turn you need to click madani before you get your mag install (which can be a dz install followed by a madani->program install for the dz discount). Typically, you will not host cards on madani the turn you install it, as it is too click intensive to install madani, host programs, and draw up to get a mag install all in the same turn.

Madani's once-per-turn restriction can be cheated similarly to The Basalt Spire's. It is very common to install a card at the end of the corp turn, then again on your turn, for example after starting a run and kk'ing to free up MU. In some cases, you may want to think further ahead and plan out the option for multiple madani installs. This can mean using madani at the end of your turn, for example to install revolver discounted with dzmz(s), so that you can install hush on the corp turn and still have your next-turn install available to respond to any ice rezzes. You don't want to end up with key programs, especially breakers, in madani jail because you need to use madani twice in a turn but can't. This comes up the most with Euler and Gauss, and is partially why propeller is in the list. In some cases, consider installing Gauss/Euler early (whichever is less relevant in the context of the corp's ice suite) to avoid madani jail situations. I've never done it but in theory with knickknack madani (or over-install console) you have a "break glass in case of emergency" button to get something out of jail so you can simulchip it in. Oh also, in the super lategame you can sell madani to kk once all the programs have come and gone (and somehow the game isn't over).

There's too much to explain everything here but I'll highlight some common play patterns.

  • Chase spins before burner so the corp can't undo your hard work with a shuffle, and so you can top agendas if desired.
  • Be aware that khusyuk also shuffles, if you plan to do burner as well in the turn, maybe do khusyuk first.
  • Speaking of shuffles, there are a lot of moon pool decks that shuffle agendas into R&D. Also, sometimes corp is obviously planning to spin back agendas which you can force with a run. Time your khusyuk's for right after this for maximum effect.
  • "Burner is Thoughtsieze". Whenever you think your opponent is about to make a play with cards in hand, or if you can't read them well just whenever possible/convenient, play burner to disrupt the corp. Nuvem/LEO pushing in the remote? Burner the seamless. R+ drawing up a ton? burner the combo pieces (yes you can bottom superconducting). Threat 4? Burner on the turn you interact vs AUco or Weyland. You will find corps tripping over themselves as their gameplans slip out of their hands, giving you the time to close.
  • Blind hush aggressively vs R+ and AUco. Click to move hush a lot.
  • Poke centrals vs Weyland to find the event horizons to hush them. If you can't force a rez or don't have the time, pre-hush on your khusyuk runs, you don't want them ETR'd. I've even used madani after passing the hushed outer ice to install muse, overwrite hush, re-install hush from heap on inner ice, just to ensure khusyuk connects.
  • Botulus at the end of the corp's turn to get 2 counters. You can beat pharos in particular this way, but of course there's plenty of applications, even if you are using it blind.
  • Follow up a burner run with a cup sweep if you expect agendas so you can see all of a normally sized HQ (those are less common these days though).
  • Click fermenter on 3 vs Ob. Don't greed to 4, they will likely mavirus purge it.
  • Consider selling Euler/Gauss, especially if on muse. It depends on the matchup, recursion available, and if you plan to make multiple runs against one server / ice type.
  • I would say 80% of the time you khusyuk for 6 2's, with another 10% for 6 1's and 10% for <6 (2's or 1's). You are more often to do undersized khusyuks in fast scrappy matchups, especially PD and R+.

There's one last trick that deserves its own paragraph: cupellation vs regenesis. You may be aware that there are a few runner cards that prevent regenesis from adding an agenda from archives to the score area by interacting with archives. Most relevant is cupellation hosting something plus any way to trash it on the corp turn (sending the hosted card to archives). Shaper has always been able to do this with simulchip, but in this deck it is trivially easy with madani as well. This forms a key part of the AUco matchup. Against a corp not trained in the dark arts, you can catch them in the act, parry their score, and steal the fujii yourself (you did your homework chasing spins/moon pools the previous turn right?). On equal footing with knowledge, there's a whole clot-esque minigame here. Corp AA's and asks for action, do you clot (trash cup hosting a card)? Make sure they didn't use AUco this turn, meaning this can't be a regenesis push. A good corp will start doing this with longevity, sericulture, hybrid release. Note, if they ask for action and you decline, they cannot score and install an asset/agenda in that server the next click as the scoring PAW has closed. They must take some other action, and if they want to install an asset/agenda it must go elsewhere. With Augustus putting charlotte into AUco (I built the same list +- 2 cards a few weeks ago, I strongly agree with that deck plan), we even have an NGO bluff parallel. How this plays out is under-explored, going into worlds we felt favored in the AUco matchup (and to my knowledge won all our AUco games), but now that the cat is out of the bag the matchup may be roughly even.

In testing we felt the deck's only bad matchup was combo PD, but even then you can win with lots of practice and a little luck. LEO may also be a bit tricky but not unwinnable. The deck is tuned for our fast meta; if things slowed down with combo PD and kingmaking R+ decks taking bans, I could see swapping joy ride for harmony AR therapy to give longevity into glacier matchups. I have a lot more to say about each specific matchup, but this is already a long post so I'll leave those details off.

Tournament Highlights

  • I did not drop a single runner game all tournament, including in the cut. The list is cracked. If you are thinking about trimming the run events, at CoS I played a version with 7 cards swapped - the burners, khusyuks, and botulus, for a dive package - and went 1-4. That should tell you all you need to know about what makes the deck work.
  • Both BBlum and I clotted regenesis plays and went on to win those AUco games. Mine was on turn 2 or 3, they came out the gate swinging and I was able to parry just in time.
  • I scored 7 points in a turn stealing basalt out of the remote, joy ride R&D to draw into 2nd khusyuk, then yum yum grab 4 more off R&D.
  • Every game I watched the corp's face show surprise then to despair then humor/acceptance as each burner and khusyuk got played. On Minstrel's stream game there's a sound byte of the commentators going "Surely you don't play around the 3rd khusyuk. [Nuka draw 3]. There it is, the third khusyuk's in hand!"
  • Every time the corp realizes you are planning to see 12 or 18 cards out of nowhere while shuffling between khusyuks.

It was great coming to worlds this time, my first. Practicing with Motherboard was great, meeting people in person was great, the support from teammates etc. was great. Seeing others love this deck as much as I do was probably my favorite part. Will it survive as a meta presence? I'm not sure, but maybe. It isn't just trying to gotcha with burner and khusyuk, even if the surprise probably juiced our numbers. I think the list is extremely tight for the current meta, but could have a little flexibility to adapt to a slower or different meta. I would love to see this deck continue to see play as the meta evolves. Oh, and shapers, play 3 burners. You've spent too long neglecting the faction's second best card.

decks.title: The Biawak-Holder - My Year in Netrunner
decks.identity_title: AU Co.: The Gold Standard in Clones
decks.author: KomodoCommodore
decks.identity_zh: 傲金公司: 克隆体的黄金标准
decks.description_html:
Okay yes I know this writeup is over a month late now. In my defence it’s been a busy month, I’ve had to do a lot of processing, and there’s so much I want to stuff into this writeup. Fair warning, this one is going to be an extremely sappy recap of EMEA, and the fairly tumultuous journey netrunner and mental health has been for me this year. Unlike my last sappy decklist, this one isn’t even a cynical ploy to get decklist of the week! Look at that, I’ve grown!

The Deck

I’ll talk about the deck first, because it’s the least important thing here. I brought this to Crown of Servers with my team ‘Beauty is in the Eye of the Biawak Holder.’ I don’t really know how or why, but over the past year I seem to have gained a reputation for liking biawak? No idea who started that rumour or why it’s so weirdly popular, but eh. For EMEA I figured, why not lean into it? So our team had a gimmick, we were all playing Unleash Biawak decks, Hello unleashing Biawak out of R+, me on Au Co, and L0velace, on Thule. If a Biawak subroutine trashed a card during a game, (including any opponent’s biawak, we didn’t discriminate) our opponent would receive one of 12 shiny Biawak badges! Made from actual NSG printed Biawaks that I definitely did not steal from a set of convention learner decks and then cut the faces off. No one knows where those cards went, they could be anywhere. You’ve got no proof!

It honestly performed better than you’d probably expect, despite some sloppy piloting from me, winning its share of games and handing out a few badges. There’s a lot of optimisation you can do to make this deck better at what it’s supposed to be, but also, you could just play a regular au co instead. This is a deck for handing out badges and having fun. Do not expect anything else.

The tumultuous personal stuff

EMEA was one of the best weekends of the year for me. I feel so privileged to have been able to attend, especially given there was a good chance I wouldn’t have made it. In the months leading up to EMEA, I was unsure if I’d have the funds to justify it. (Gigantic thanks to Ish and Dreadmaw, and everyone that bought a ticket for the Road to Nottingham online events, without that support I could not have attended.) And then in the weeks leading up to EMEA, I was unsure if I’d still be alive.

Turns out a major mental health crisis really impacts your ability to go to netrunner events. Who knew? I won’t go into it much, in short: a series of unfortunate life events over a month led to a significant downward spiral. By the end of it, I’d pinned my hopes of recovery on the outcome of a job interview. If I got the job, everything would be okay, if I didn’t… well. Better left unsaid.

Three days before EMEA I got the job offer. My mental health snapped back into place with the baffling grace of a derailed train crashing into a rock and bouncing right back onto the track. Narrowly avoiding being sent careening off the edge of a nearby mountain, where upon reaching the bottom it explodes comedically. If you saw me at EMEA and noticed I had an unusual amount of energy or just generally perkier than I normally am at tournaments? It’s because I genuinely didn’t believe I’d make it.

As you can gather, this year has been a rocky one for me. Both in general terms, life circumstances, mental health, and in netrunner terms. It’s pretty fair to say that getting into Netrunner last year has been one of the best things to ever happen to me. I’ve made new, wonderful friends, it got me a partner, it’s changed my perception of myself and my confidence in a myriad of positive ways. I love this game, I love this community.

But it’s also been responsible for some insecurities, crashouts, and all around not great times. The Netrunner scene, particularly in the UK, is one that is built around tournaments. I love tournaments, I love travelling around the country, getting to meet and connect with players outside of my locals, unfortunately, tournaments don’t love me. The pressure of ‘wanting to do well’ got to me. And most tournaments I attended this year, even the ones where I did achieve a decent result, left me drained, exhausted and somewhat miserable. Bubbling out of a top cut happened enough times that it became a gut punch, rather than an achievement.

I never regretted going to a tournament. But during an event, it’s pretty hard to say I was having ‘fun’. And by the end, I was generally too drained to enjoy people’s company. I was assaulted on all sides by concerned looks, friends attempting to check in, worried if I was okay. I brushed them off. Feeling bad was just the price of a tournament right? I’d enjoy them more when I got better at the game.

Unfortunately, my attempts to improve were frustrated by hitting what felt like an impenetrable ceiling. Without self-deprecation, I can confidently say I’m a perfectly okay player. One who had reached the limits of what self-directed improvement, jnet games, and replay reviews could really achieve. I couldn’t figure out how to improve, and that only made the pressure to perform more intense. I knew it was the wrong attitude to approach events with, but I couldn’t figure out how to change it.

Enter Commentary.

Parallel to this, I’d started doing the occasional commentary for online events. This started when Ams came to me, searching for a co-caster for an early Vantage Point AMT. At this point in time, I had a small web of insecurities where I didn’t feel like I was ‘allowed’ to have opinions about the game. That I was too new, not a good enough player, to talk about matchup spreads, card slots, the meta. Even in casual conversation I was somewhat scared to speak up. What if I said something wrong? What if a card I thought was performant was considered bad? What if an actually good player disagreed with me? So the idea of commentating an event was anathema. Ridiculous. Impossible

I seem to recall the conversation going like this

Ams: Hey come do commentary with me

Komodo: Uh, no. I’d be terrible at it, I’m not a good enough player, and I’m really bad at improvisation.

Ams: It’s a totally different skillset to playing netrunner, and we have good chemistry, it’s just a conversation.

Komodo: Sorry I really think I’d be bad at this, I don’t know enough. you’ll have to find someone else.

Ams: Please?

Komodo: No.

So I commentated the AMT.

That sudden 180 thanks to Laura_42. During a QTM testing session where we were spectating jnet games, we organically slipped into mock-casting them. Turns out there’s just a switch in my head that puts me into ‘caster mode’. All I had to do was flick it. In front of a microphone all of those fears, those anxieties that I didn’t know anything, that I wasn’t good enough, that I couldn’t talk without a script in front of me, they disappeared. The past 6 months of hyperfixation took over, spilled out, and I realised I was much better equipped to talk about netrunner then I ever believed.

Laura seemed to recognise this, and suggested I should try actual commentary. So I went back to Ams, hat in hand, and said:

“okay fine I’ll do it. But just this once. And nobody better be watching.”

Something like that anyway. That one silly conversation is why my voice has plagued so many tournament streams this year. So if you don’t like my casting, you know who to blame.

When the form requesting volunteer submissions for EMEA came out, I’d casted twice and had a lot of fun, but I hadn’t fully recognised just how toxic my relationship towards tournaments was becoming. So the decision to volunteer to commentate was a difficult one. I’d be giving up my chance to play, to do well. Something I at the time desperately wanted, despite part of me knowing just how unrealistic it was. In the end I said to hell with it, applied to do comms, and left the decision in the hands of the organisers, figuring they probably wouldn’t want someone so inexperienced anyway.

That’s one of the best netrunner decisions I made.

Enter EMEA.

By the time EMEA rolled around, I had a few more tournaments under my belt, and after a large crashout at Bristol Megacities, and the realisation that spending the second day at a weird immersive art museum thing with my partner was 100 times more fun than making top cut would have been, I was no longer torn about my decision to volunteer for EMEA. For the first time ever, I walked into a netrunner tournament wholly unstressed. On Friday my performance would be measured not by how well I played, but how many Biawaks my team rezzed. For the main event, the only thing I worried about was how good my outfit was. (pretty fucking good if I say so myself)

No last minute anxieties over deck slots, no dread at seeing me matched with a notable player, no self-flagelatting over missed lines or silly mistakes. All I had to do was pretend I know what I’m talking about, and overconfidence in front of a microphone? That I have in spades. It wasn’t easy, there were myriad tech issues to contend with, staff sickness threw our stream schedule totally out of whack, all the trains home on Sunday were cancelled! And despite that, I had a great time. We fixed what we could, worked around what we couldn’t. For once, the stress of an event was manageable instead of debilitating.

It was fantastic. This was the first tournament I attended where I can say I just… had fun. The first tournament where I actually got to enjoy post-event drinks at the pub, where I could wander around between rounds and not feel the crushing weight of a lost games, or even worse, the mounting pressure of a win streak. It’s the first event where I really felt like I was a person, where I felt like myself.

It took a year, but EMEA was where I finally felt like I’d found my place in Netrunner. It was an exhausting, manic weekend, one I survived solely due to overzealous consumption of apple juice, sweets, and good vibes. It’s reframed my approach to this game, and going forward I’m hoping to have a much healthier relationship with the scene. I still want to improve, but going forward there’ll maybe be a little less self flagellation and a few more silly youtube videos.

Thank yous

There’s too many people to mention all of them by name, but I’m going to try damnit.

  • Ish & Dreadmaw: You ran an incredibly smooth event, despite myriad technical issues you kept things running with frankly obscene levels of class and patience. You made sure we were supported, and built a truly incredible atmosphere.

  • Ams: You put my voice in a video game and my face on a card. You helped me uncover talents I never dreamed I had, I’m so lucky to be able to consider you my friend.

  • Extrac: You’re an absolutely wonderful co-caster and a joy to be around. You lent me energy when I was flagging, and seamlessly covered for me any time I got tongue-tied. I’m forever grateful for you letting me crash at yours when my train home was cancelled. We’re going to defend our title of ‘best dressed stream-team’ to the death.

  • Harmonbee: One of my few equals in the all-important Netrunner fashion contest. Our conversations on tournament mental really helped me realise just where I’d been going wrong this year. And that top cut burrito spared everyone the headache of me passing out mid-livestream. All the work you did behind the scenes was incredibly appreciated

  • Hello: Your R+ rezzed more Biawaks and handed out more badges than me and L0velace combined. You’re one of the kindest, most genuine people I know.

  • Cobalt, tuno, & Wowarlock: You stepped in at short notice to give me and Extrac much needed breaks with some wonderful comms. The health of my throat thanks you.

  • Everyone in the Midlands scene. I couldn’t ask for a better gang of people. Our meetups are still the highlights of my week

  • Ariel & Maninthemoon: Letting me paint gorgeous tokens to destress between top cut rounds, and for all the work you do on showdowns. The effort you put into netrunner events is staggering, also. Maninthemoon can do a backflip. It’s sick.

  • Baa Ram Wuu: You gave me some kind words when I really needed them, and for being consistently great fun both to play against and to cast.

  • Cobrabubbles and Rad.andro: We didn’t speak much, but after matching into you during CoS I totally stole part of your makeup look for the rest of the weekend.

  • Any volunteers that helped with stream setup, especially spotting. You made us seem so much better informed than we actually are.

  • Anyone in stream chat who said nice things about my outfits. You know who you are.

  • L0velace: I love you. Your support for me this year has been nothing less than spectacular. You were there for me at my lowest and celebrated me at my highest. I don’t have enough words to say just how much you mean to me, how incredible, and wonderful, and downright fantastic you are. I’m so proud of you for everything you achieved this year, both in and out of netrunner. You TOd an excellent CTK, you took my Biawak Melies to 3rd place at a megacity, you made top cut at EMEA! I refuse to apologise for the torment you’ve suffered from my gradual decline into ‘Content Creator’, or for my being unable to turn off ‘caster-mode’ during an intimate dinner on the saturday night. Netrunner is one of the best things to have happened to me this year. You’re even better. You’re the Greenmail to my Biawak. The Sisyphus to my Cloud Eater. The rolled eyes to my strained and cliche netrunner analogies. You mean the world to me.

So yeah. I’ve been playing Netrunner for a little over a year now. If you told me back then that in that time I’d have a new girlfriend, have voice acted in a video game, casted multiple major events, and started making youtube videos… To be honest, it’s still hard to believe now. Sure it’s hardly been all roses, but I wouldn’t trade it for the world.

Join me in 6 months when I release another sappy decklist writeup about some new terribly unbelievable thing that happened to me because of netrunner or something.

My book is out!

A lot of people have messaged me in the past weeks asking where they can get my book about Ob Superheavy Logistics: Extract. Export. Excel.. It's out NOW, so let's get that out of the way:

I want a paperback

You can get a paperback copy HERE. It's printed by lulu.com, a print-on-demand service. One person has asked me to print hardcover, but I don't want to go through the trouble to do design work for that, print proofs, and then print it at a high cost unless I know there's wider interest.

I want a PDF

You can get a PDF copy HERE, from itch.io. It's free, or you can make a donation if you want. The book is under a Creative Commons license, so feel free to share the file around if you want to.

The sappy part

Writing this book was a big endeavour. It was way bigger than any personal project I've ever worked on, and I think people have complimented it enough that I am finally very proud of the result. Here are a few things I learned while making it:

  • I will never get over how terrifying making something is. No matter how hard you work at it, it's going to be full of gaps and errors, enough for you to constantly doubt whether the whole idea is worth it.
  • Still working on something despite the doubt requires a lot of support from everyone around you. A lot of people helped in all the stages of materially making this book happen, and a lot more helped by encouraging me and reminding me that what I was doing was worthwhile.
  • This thing is a lot harder to do if you're the first person ever quite doing it, and you have to invent a lot of things about how it's done. Having to make up words all by myself is tough! NRDB writeups are great, but Netrunner really lacks more people who want to write theory about it. I hope this book inspires people to write articles, blogs, books, whatever they want. I know how difficult it can be to find the motivation for it, especially when you don't know how to go about getting your writing out. If you want help or support, reach out to me, I want to help.

Red Room Ob

When Svyatogor Excavator was unbanned, I saw that SCRUBS were already iterating on my Phat Ob list, so I set out to do something different. A conspiracy was quickly born to make Red Room Ob happen, in an attempt to bring it to all Continentals.

My Red Roommates did a great job. Thank you to New Puldrix, Otra, Spidz, AceEmpress, Avi, Bluestar, l0velace, Lady Duckland, Nova, and zhae, for iterating on this deck until we got even more confused about what it was. Also thank you to laura and protheseus, who joined us just to help with Shaper and Esa testing. Special congratulations to cablooshe, who joined the conspiracy, then built a completely different version of the deck on her own, and ended up 2nd place at American Continentals with it!

What I'm publishing here is just the version of the deck that I brought to EMEA 2026. In practice, the deck can be built in a lot of different ways: you can play anywhere from 49 to 64 cards, you can play no 3-pointers or no 1-pointers, you can play Measured Response or just be fair. We have tested, and sometimes brought to tournaments, cards such as Humanoid Resources, Reduced Service, Manegarm Skunkworks, Let Them Dream, Mestnichestvo, Tocsin, Kessleroid, Flagship, The Powers That Be, and more. You can sort of do anything with this pile, The Red Room will carry you; play two copies if you want.

Because we can't even agree on how to build the deck, I won't give play advice, except for one very important thing: expend Eminent Domain. Play Armed Asset Protection. Get your Mdom stolen for a Red Room counter. Money is good.

I expect further variations of this to show up at Worlds; I have no idea what they will look like. Be afraid.
