decks.description_html:
Preamble

First things first, should you play this deck? Generally, I fear unfortunately the answer is probably not. If you're interested in getting the highest win rate for your efforts, you'll genuinely be better served with any of the other currently competitive corps. The play patterns necessary for this deck are very sharp, require a lot of practice and mental exertion and even small inaccuracies can cost double digit win percentage. Additionally, the meta has just become incredibly hostile to this deck. Out of the 18 matches mentioned in the title not a single one was against shaper, the easiest matchup, and instead all were either against runners with Hermes or Audrey v2, sometimes both. Fighting for your life in every corp game of an 11 round tournament is not as fun as it sounds, and it doesn't sound very fun to begin with.

There is a reward for putting disproportionate effort into it though, as this deck has consistently averaged a 5-1 winrate for me for quite a while and now for wowarlok too, who also brought this list to EMEA online continentals. That is basically as good as you're going to get in Netrunner. That is roughly the same odds as losing to the runner finding 9 points in 12 accesses or as all three of your Fully Operational(FlOp) being in the bottom half of the deck. So if you're interested in a deck that has possibly the most intricate lines in current Netrunner and is incredibly receptive to skill expression (even if I say so myself), this might be a deck for you.

I've dreaded this writeup for a while now, but with my continental season over I have no excuse for procrastinating any longer. The cause of my bittersweet feelings is that this is likely to be my last entry in the FtM PD development journey, which has gripped me for the last four months. At this point though I consider the deck to be basically 95% correct and I also don't want to get stuck playing one corp in a meta that is moving on.

As such it is a good time to pull everything together and explain the insights gained along the way. I consider CyberSharks writeup of Twink Shipping to be so good as to possible serve as the canonical example of explaining a deck. I hope to be able to replicate a fraction of that here.

History

Flood the Market(FtM) was released with Vantage Point and the first list to put all the now key pieces together was The Deck That Makes You Trans by Lunari. As far as I know, Méliès City Luxury Line(Train) hadn't been released at that point and the FtM score 9 in one turn line not yet discovered.

Credit for the first explicit mention of the full synergy of FtM, Train, Wage Workers(WW), The Powers That Be(TPTB) and Synchrocyclotron(Synchro) seems to go to Yi Sun in their Homage to Tuno's Wellness Check. I had not become aware of their list until relatively recently though. At this point I'm however perfectly ready to believe that all of Netrunner deckbuilding is just a variation of something Tuno has tried before. As an aside, its book has come out. I got my preorder copy at EMEA and can highly recommend buying one!

Of course the first time FtM PD was catapulted to prominence was by liadahlia, when she brought Trains Rights! to APAC, winning the Showdown in amazing style. Importantly, the deck established the concept of winning through relentless rush, the operative quote of the writeup for me being "Win on turn 8".

My first contact with that list was when local SCRUBS member Dasuiwa brought it to Münster districts and I was suddenly forced to find a way to dismantle it to make cut. Luckily Seb was busted at the time and I barely managed to. That game left an impression on me though.

Shortly thereafter, FtM PD caused its first political prisoner, with the otherwise innocent Offworld Office(OffOff) landing on the 26.05 banlist, where it remains to this day, justified or not. With my beloved Ob having been similarly hit, I ended up in search of a new corp.

Naturally people gave up on FtM PD, and it seemed to have been relegated to jank(note the subtle 48 cards) status. Luckily I saw Jtfq99999 perform with the deck on jnet and realized, there was still something there.

With the more ambitious goal of win on turn 6 in mind, I ended up developing and grinding the deck for the Summer showdown. This lead to the first iteration of High Speed Rail. After being unexpectedly successful with the list, I kept refining it, leading to respectable showings at:

  • High Speed Rail 2.0 America AMT
  • High Speed Rail 2.1 Winterthur Megacity
  • High Speed Rail 2.2 Hasselt Megacity

For reasons entirely unrelated to this particular deck, after Megacity season Red Level Clearance(RLC) ended up on the 26.08 banlist. It will probably remain there for quite a while, for reasons to be explored soon. Suffice to say, Plutus is even sadder now than he already was before. My FtM PD was only on two copies anyways though, and half the time I used those for econ, so the hit wasn't as hard. In a sensible naming scheme this should nonetheless have warranted a mayor revision, but the next version ended up as:

  • High Speed Rail 2.3

So now we are in the unfortunate situation where the only change between 2.3 and 3.0 is the relatively minor:

  • 2x Regolith Mining License(RML) -> 2x Humanoid Resources(HR): HR on turn 2 or 3 just moves the game plan forward so much more than Regolith that it's downsides are acceptable.

Modelling

For the moment, we'll just assume that the only win condition of our deck is firing FtM three times with 5 remotes filled each time to score a 3pt agenda each time. This will be justified later on, in deckbuilding considerations. To understand the constraints behind pulling off the combo, we'll consider increasingly sophisticated models for getting to the score.

At base level we need

  • 5 ice,
  • 7 root installables (3 of which are are agendas) and
  • FtM (which we recur with the PD ability).

That's only 13 cards, 12 installs 9 credits and 3 double operations.

To start off, let's consider how long it would take us under optimal conditions to set this up with only basic actions. 12 install, 4 credits and 3 doubles puts us at 22 clicks, so 8 turns. In that time we draw the required number of cards through mandatory draw (with a perfectly stacked deck), so no need to click for it.

Clicking for 4 credits is really slow though, when Hedge Fund(HF) exists. With HF we can compress obtaining the 4c into one operation click, getting us down to 19 clicks, at the price of needing another card. So now we'd need to click for draw twice, because we're missing out on a mandatory draw by being faster. That brings us back to 21 clicks, which is however overall still a turn less!

For another example, if we have WW available we might theoretically be able to got up to 33% faster. Only now the discrete structure of turns actually matters. With WW as one of the installables we can

  • turn 1 install & rez WW, two installs, draw
  • turn 2&3 triple install, credit
  • turn 4 quadruple credit
  • turn 5&6&7 install, FtM

Note that we're not able to get any WW value for the last three turns because of the clunkiness of doubles. But again, we save a click and thereby a turn over having just basic actions.

The point of this exercise is to show:

  1. That we can accelerate our game plan through card effects, specifically operations and assets.
  2. That draw, installs, credits and playing operations are important quantities which we can trade off for one another through the effect of our cards.
  3. That scoring out on turn 6 might not be as unrealistic as it might seem at first with 3x3point agendas.

We'll start with cards that discount installs, because there are so few:

  • RLC: 1 card and 1 credit for 1 install, clicklessly is, with the benefit of hindsight pretty busted and was just waiting to be exploited.
  • Top-Down Solutions(TDS): 2 credit for +1 card and 2 installs in one operation compresses what would otherwise be an entire turn with basic operations into a single click. Importantly it reduces the cost of an install to half a click. I think it is no understatement to say that this card is also busted, but in a more subtle way.
  • WW: For 2 credits and 1 install we can reduce the cost of 3 installs to 2 clicks, repeatedly. So an install is only 0.66 clicks with WW.
  • TPTB: For 1 credit we get up to 2 clickless installs, and importantly can do so also from archives. A power that significantly extends our reach, for example by being able to score agendas from archives.
  • Active Policing, KPI, Greasing the Palm, Peer Review: 1 card and 1 click for 1 install, with minor side benefits. Not actually click compressing though.
  • Warm Reception, Mercia B4LL4RD: 1 install for theoretically 1 free install per turn. When these inevitably get trashed after firing once though, we are left with 1 install for 1 install, only now with time delay.

Importantly, operations can combine with WW to compress clicks even more. An install of a TDS in a triple operation WW turn actually only comes in at 0.33 clicks. Similarly, Synchro can not just half the click cost of a double, but enable us to play it in the same turn as two other operations with WW, bringing a double operations down to 0.66 clicks.

There are plenty of cards which give a combination of draw and credits. For the most important ones, consult the chart:

It should come as no surprise that FlOp is literally off the chart. At its top end, with 5 servers, it reduces the value of a credit or draw to ~1/10th of a click. As such, it is the key card of our mid and late game econ and being able to recur it is very strong.

There are of course two very unrealistic assumptions we've made so far.

  1. We can stack the deck to draw exactly the cards needed.
  2. Our opponent let's us do what we want without interacting.

We can tackle the first of these with math. The most important concept from statistics for Netrunner is of course the hypergeometric distribution. It models the process of drawing without replacement, which is exactly what we engage in whenever we draw a card from the deck. Using it, we can calculate the probability of finding a card we have a certain amount of after a certain number of draws:

(Note that the k=3 line also gives the probability for the runner to win on that number of accesses)

(If we could find the slots for it, an 11th ice would possibly still be good)

Of course these are not actually independent. For example, when we draw more ice than expected, the probability to also draw our FtM goes down. With the multivariate hypergeometric distribution we can calculate such combined probabilities. I'll abbreviate the details here and just give the most pertinent graph:

So we should actually expect to have to see 25-31 cards to assemble all our pieces. Hence, we'll need a lot more draw relative to the stacked deck examples from before. This also implies however that we have quite a bit of redundancy to work with in our deck, 16 cards on average. We'll come back to that fact when we discuss matchups.

The second assumptions is way harder to make explicit, because the ways runners can and are trying to disrupt our gameplan are so varied. Ranging from accesses, trashing, bouncing cards, econ denial, sabotage, nothing is really of the table. Therefore I have significantly less of an explicit model here and am more reliant on arguments and intuition. Fundamentally, the ways to inhibit the runner fit into a few categories:

  1. Click denial: Every turn we're able to score out quicker denies the runner at least 4 clicks.
  2. Econ overload: Our important assets cost 3&4 to trash and can come back both quickly and many times over.
  3. Access denial: Ice increases the cost per access and can help reduce them to a tolerable amount.

Deck Building

Agenda Suite

The 6x3pts agenda suite is of course a notorious staple of the 40 card ids because it used to have the highest number of necessary accesses before the release of Let Them Dream(LtD). Now that title goes to a (3,3,3) combination, with 3 LtDs. But the difference is only 0.7 accesses on average and in particular any higher access agenda suite needs to spend 3 influence for LtDs. So there are really 4 reasons why 6x3pts is the only sensible option here at the moment:

  1. It maximizes the number of accesses needed without disproportionate influence spend.
  2. It uses the least possible number of slots, which are extra valuable in this deck.
  3. It is not significantly more difficult for us to score a 5/3 than a 4/2, since we have to score one 5/3 in each 3 scores setup anyways.
  4. There are no 4/2s whose upsides outweigh their downsides on the last 3 points. (OffOff might, but is banned of course.)

Once we have committed to that agenda suite we obviously play 3 trains. Send a Message(SaM) is included for a lack of alternatives. It's rare that we get much value from scoring it. If anything we mostly take the free rez when it gets stolen. Salvo Testing does nothing for us and Vulnerability Audit is actively harmful to our scoring plan.

Assets

  • 3 of each Spin Doctor(SD) and WW is clearly non-negotiable.
  • TPTB fires at most twice in the game, but when it does it provides so much value at such low cost that having it is well worth it. If we are going to play it, we should play two, because we are bound to lose or not find one of them.
  • Synchro is somewhat more dubious. If we're only planning to use it to discount FtM then it will probably only save 1 or 2 clicks all game, which is questionable value for a rez cost of 3. There are some side benefits with WW, such as triple install FtM, score of course. But in that case it could probably be a one of. Its saving grace is really Corporate Hospitality, which we'll discuss in a moment. Because it creates so much more value in combination with that card, it becomes reasonable to include it as 3x, to have it available in the mid game.
  • HR is the most flexible slot in this deck, ironically because of how quickly it becomes obsolete in our game plan. Its role is primarily to stabilize the early game. If I could fire a HR turn 2, I would every time, but it soon becomes just too slow thereafter.
  • RML is another card to stabilize the early game. In theory it combos with WW, but in practice this rarely happens. Unfortunately it usually also is just too slow. If we click it 3 times turn 2 we've made a nice +7 credits, but we're also almost a turn behind where we could be if it had been a HR. One factor in its favor is the higher trash cost, which exerts the runner more in dealing with it.
  • Bass CH1R180G4: This card seems tempting and I've played with him as well, but the fundamental problem is that he doesn't really gain us clicks. He turns an install into a click at the price of 3c. We have however preciously few ways of discounting installs. Usually this unfortunately turns out to be a bad trade.
  • Warm Reception has an amazing payoff when it installs a card and derezzes a Spin Doctor, or stays on board iced for multiple turns. Unfortunately this usually doesn't happen exactly in the matchups where we'd need it to happen the most. The risk profile of this card is just too unfavorable in the current meta.
  • Gaslight: there are some times where it comes in handy, even later in the game getting it back with TPTB to summon the other FtM for example. However it's -1 install and gets trashed relatively cheaply. Most importantly though, the only realistic slot I could make for it is cutting a HR, which again, I feel gives more value in the same situation.
  • Nico Campaign/Otto Campaign: Looks cute, but the money is kinda slow, they get trashed relatively cheaply and even if they do run to completion leave us with -1 install.

Operations

  • 2 FtM, 3 FlOps, 3 TDS are also non-negotiable.
  • 1 Nanomanagement extends our range in the mid and endgame to such a degree as to be well worth the slot. In particular it can be incredibly useful to get both the operation and install click from WW, even without any other click gainer.
  • Corporate Hospitality(CH) is somewhat mid on it's own, maybe something we'd play on turn 2 for lack of alternatives. However it becomes incredible in the midgame. With Synchro rezzed we not only get 2 draw 2 credits for a click, but also our most important card back from archives. This is usually FlOp, TDS or another CH, sometimes an asset. That further accelerates our gameplan and enables incredible turns. Getting to the 7c required to rez Synchro and play CH is often a key objective of the first 3 turns. In the scoring turns it interferes with FtM, so we often end up unable to slot the third copy in. I still maintain it's necessary to play 3x in order to have access early enough and because they unfortunately have a habit of getting trashed quite cheaply.
  • Predictive Planogram(PP) is an incredible card and probably still underrated. It's not only an unrestricted Ritual for the corp, which can be invaluable to draw into the next draw card in the early game, but also optional economy with a tag punishment mode. And most importantly all that from 0 credits. The degree to which this card stabilizes the early game if drawn is not to be dismissed. That fixes it at 3x in my opinion.
  • Your Digital Life seems really tempting, especially with the increased hand size of the ID. It is of course one the cards that busted by being unrestricted in its upside. However, I have to agree 100% with liadahlia's take on it. My problem is that the play patterns that enable it are actively harmful to our deck. In the opening hand it also only gains us 3c. If we draw to improve that we've now allocated two clicks to it and thereby almost halved the payoff. If we hold back our Spin Doctors to draw next turn we miss out on cards that could've given us more tempo, if we overdraw with FlOp we have to discard valuables afterwards. And most importantly, it doesn't draw us cards itself or recovers us from a Transfer of Wealth.

ICE

The purpose of our ice, beside making servers operational, is to as best as possible prevent the runner from slowing us down. This is a contradiction of course, because rezzing any ice inherently slows us down. That is especially true in the early game, where the click-value of credits is still high. Hence we are looking for the cheapest possible ice with the highest possible payoff.

Consider Drafter for example. The ice obviously doesn't do much before there are valuable cards in archives. If the runner disrespects it however we could easily get a PP back to hand and a free install, possibly of the asset they have just invested resources in trashing. This trade is actually in our favor. We can now spend the click we would have on installing that asset on the PP instead, getting us back to our original credits. The runner on the other hand has just "lost" a click, the resources he spend on trashing (potentially up to 4c with WW) and given us a rezzed ice. Especially later in the game, the threat of getting another FlOp back into hand is so great as to almost make facechecking without a killer impossible. Therefore the ambiguity of whether any particular unrezzed ice could be a Drafter is one of our greatest deterrents. For all that, Drafter is well justified at a rez cost of 3.

Ablative Barrier(AB) is in a weird spot, because on the one hand it is just a cheap gear check, but on the other hand we'd really prefer not to rez it before threat 3 so as to get the most out of its effect. Here the Drafter ambiguity works in our favor. Of course that also has the advantage that if we get an agenda stolen early we can more easily bounce back. Especially in the late game though, AB presents a significant challenge to our opponent clearing the board to prevent us from making another score. Also, there are limited options in faction for good cheap ice. The cost difference between 2c and 3c might not sound like a lot, but that can quite literally end up costing us a click at first, and then ultimately a turn. Because it is so porous, both in the early and late game though, it's fine to only run 2 of them. There is a cute line of putting a SaM behind it and using that to rez AB when it gets stolen, but this is generally not worth it, if avoidable.

Code gates are the forte of HB and Scatter Field is a particularly mean example of that. Because we're not planning to double ice any server, it usually ends up as a 3 cost rez that takes the runner 4 to break. Even the facecheck can be highly beneficial for us, because we get an install out of it, which is again almost worth an entire click. This justifies its increased cost over Whitespace, which can often end up to porous and breaks to cheaply once a decoder is out.

A one of Flyswatter is useful into anarch running Fermenter or Audrey and it is a cheap hard EtR. It increases the ambiguity of facechecking, but we should be under no illusions that this is going to effect much of a lockout.

Now if we revisit the previous choices, it turns out that we pretty much have 14 influence locked in stone. So the question becomes what is the most useful thing we can do with one influence. I think the answer to that, surprisingly, is Tree Line. Obviously on a remote server a Tree Line is just a Palisade where you have to hope that the facecheck refunds you the difference. The matchup I'm most concerned about though is against crim, because of ToWs ability to disrupt the early game massively. The problem is, crim figures out at some point that the only realistic EtR on HQ is a code gate, since you don't want to rez AB before threat or Drafter with empty archive. So Tree Line adds some defense here because it adds ambiguity and also makes ToW only credit neutral for the runner. Case in point, Tree Line breaks for 4 credits with Curupira and Rising Tide. (It can also be used to defend R&D from easy runs by the same logic.) Arguably Kessleroid could also be played in this slot though.

Hagen is another popular choice but suffers from being to expensive for the early game. It does offer some protection against reg breakers there, but becomes bad once a suite of them is out. It doesn't do enough against ice cheating approaches though. It has the same breaking point for Audrey as Tree Line and falls just as much to Botulus or Boomerang. The fact that Drafter scares non reg runners off from facechecking without counters/Simulchips makes its first subroutine barely ever relevant.

Rush vs Attrition

This PD list is of course not the only one with FtM to have done well at EMEA. Also into top cut with good results made it:

  • Kikai with Tiered Flud PD
  • Rubenpieters with Tree Lines will continue until morale improves

Obviously these lists made some quite distinct slot choices. I would like to contribute my thoughts on the difference in perspective that might have motivated that.

As articulated before, I fundamentally believe in rush. If we can threaten to score out on turn 6 it puts the runners on an incredibly mean clock and fundamentally changes the value of their cards and what tools they have access to. In 5 runner turns a turn 1 companion only nets as much money as a Sure Gamble, but doesn't do so instantly. A Daily Casts installed on turn 2 might not pay out completely before the game is over. With 20 clicks, even if the runner finds 2 Dr. Nuka Vrolyck's and dedicated 6 clicks to using them, they'll only see 17 cards of their deck in total. If they have 3 ToW in there they should expect to only find one of them. Most likely this will not be enough time for them to find and install all their breakers, and if they do it will be a significant investment. The Twinning will not accumulate enough power counters for more than one multiaccess in that time. Because the runner doesn't have access to an exponential curve on their economy the same way we do, there is a good chance we can score out before they're properly set up. And any agenda in the score area is not only safe, but makes it much harder to find the remaining ones. We'll absolutely peak, run out of resources and fall of, but ideally only after we've already won the game. In this view, we're heavily betting on the click-denial strategy we've identified earlier.

An alternative viewpoint to this is what I'd call attrition, or the econ-denial strategy from earlier. The theory here being that if we can put enough costly assets behind costly ice we'll eventually be able to create a board state from which we can start scoring agendas. I believe playing Tiered Subscription(TS) is a perfect example of this difference in perspective. If we intend to score out on turn 6 we would expect to at absolutely most get 5 credits out of it, if we found it turn 1 and the runner ran every time. It is an asset the runner should not bother thrashing in that situation because it does not meaningfully speed up the game plan. If we do expect the game to go to turn 10-12 however, that math changes. Then TS gives a meaningful amount of credits and the runner has to deal with it, preferably early. Another example is Sleipnir, an undeniably very strong ice. It's increased rez cost come with a tempo hit though, it breaks for the same as Scatter Field, because the draw can usually be allowed, and a face check does not advance our game plan right now. Getting a card back into the deck is only meaningful when you expect to play long enough to draw and us it again. In a more attrition oriented game plan, that is the case. Another card that makes a lot more sense in an attrition rather than rush posture is RML. Oftentimes you don't even take the last 3 credits and pose it as a challenge to the runner instead to clear that server.

Kikai has very precisely identified the ways a runner can win against FtM PD:

  1. control the board
  2. take central accesses

I believe the reason this list has performed the most consistent out of FtM PD decks so far is that both of these factors get worse for the corp the longer the game goes on. This is especially the case in the problem matchups, Seb, Mercury and Virus Loup. In the end, we're playing a 44 card deck and by the time we have gone through it, the runner is likely to have half the gas in their tank left. That just doesn't bode well for us.

Game Plan

We've gone over what we need to win in the modeling chapter. It sounds simplistic, but generally we want to play the lines that get us towards this goal the fastest.

Consider mulligan on hands with two agendas or more, or a lack of tempo cards. A good opening hand should have a HR+ice, PP or Spin Doctor to draw us into more cards. Whenever we have to take basic actions that are not install or operation we're basically losing tempo.

Turn 1 is when we are the most vulnerable. If we have to expect ToW we can consider icing HQ, holding a PP in reserve for recovery or dumping enough assets on the board to potentially duck it. This can include taking relatively aggressive triple install WW lines early for example. Generally we want to start getting remotes up and installing is one of the less tempo bad things we can do at this point. We want to avoid clicking for credit or draw here, although the second one can be acceptable.

Turn 2 we should get 2-3 remotes fully operational here, our credits might still be low at this point, but we're getting ready to play our first FlOp at the end of this or start of next turn. If we can get a HR to fire it's a lot of good tempo here.

Turn 3 we start pulling value out of our assets, depending on our draw we're in a position to take triple install/operation WW turns or play FlOp to get the money to rez Synchro, play CH and get FlOp back.

Turn 4 we should end the turn at 4~ish fully operational servers, and can start seriously getting our money up with FlOp.

Turn 5 we should complete our set of 5 servers. Potentially we can score the first agenda here already, but it's generally better to only do this when it is somewhat tempo positive, for example because we get a missing WW back with TPTB.

Turn 6 we should ideally be in a position to score out here by completing the remaining points. If we're note it often makes little sense to overextend ourselves. If we can get into a more secure position for a turn later that's just as fine.

It bears reiterating, on a fully set up board (with Synchro rezzed), we can score out very easily for 10c. Rez TPTB, FtM score train, install train with TPTB, get FtM back, FtM score train, install agenda with TPTB, FtM score to 9. With WW we can add in an operation for free. Importantly, we don't need WW to start scoring, we can get him back with TPTB before we take the first action thrice. Generally WW is most important in the early game, Synchro in the mid and endgame and TPTB only in the endgame. Theoretically we can also score with only 4 servers by manually advancing, or even score an unadvanced agenda off the board with Nano and WW, but these lines are usually suboptimal in actual play and only serve for closing the game or urgently removing a known agenda.

Very important factors to also seriously consider when playing this list is the necessity of rezzing ice and the use of recursion.

  • On any particular run, it is not worth rezzing the ice if it puts us into a worse position than the runner. Especially in the beginning it is easy to bottom out this way and lose tempo recovering.
  • With SD/CH/PDs Id/TPTB we can potentially bring up to 12 cards back into the game. That should allow us to fire 5 FlOp in the average game, which is just incredible value.

If you fishbulb this list to practice, you might even get there already on turn 5. Generally, the runner is going to work on not making this gameplan work out like that though. Oftentimes the runner can delay some of these steps enough that we go into turn 7. If they install Hermes you should expect to probably need another additional turn more.

Matchups

Mercury

Very strange matchup, where not a lot of opposition can happen for a while. Then they find an agenda on a dig, Hermes bounce and/or Reprise a card, steal a second agenda, and suddenly you're in big trouble. Mercury gets a lot better at threat 4, so it's generally preferable to pursue a 3+6 scoring pattern. Not icing centrals is not really an option, because we'd lose too many accesses on R&D and HQ. Agendas will generally be safer on the board. Our most important ice are going to be Scatter Field and Tree Line, everything else can get bypassed by Malandragem.

MuslihaT

The uncomfortable part about MuslihaT is that she can open into hands with which she could make +14c on turn 1. That makes economically taxing her very difficult early on. Expect to mostly get run over for the first few turns. MuslihaTs weakness, ironically, is draw. After an initial burst she might genuinely run out of cards and drop off, giving us more of a window to set up. If we miss that window and she gets full breakers up none of our ice is really taxing for her though and her ability to get multi access going becomes problematic.

Esa

I'd rate this as one of the easier matchups. Our code gates do work, our cheap barriers forces xir to find Rising Tide, and xi doesn't like breaking our Drafters either. There is always the chance to get unlucky on sabotage, but generally we have enough recursion and redundancy. We have to aggressively spin back key combo pieces though. Fun lines are bringing back a sabotaged SD with AB, or even just putting an AB on archives preemptively.

Seb

Super challenging matchup because of the combination of Audrey, ToW and ice destruction. Our best chances are that Seb can be slow to setup and doesn't actually make enough money to endlessly keep trashing assets. At some point we'll have to ice archives. Seb get's an incredible amount of value from threat 3, so we should try to avoid that if possible. So a 6+3 scoring pattern is preferable, where we probably have to be ready to entirely repair the board after the first scoring turn. It's also very important to either force Seb to not float tags at all or only play PP when we get to fire both modes.

Virus Loup

Start with the assumption you're going to lose. None of our ice holds up to Audrey, or Botulus. It is hard to economically tax him, because he gets value and tempo from trashing. Purging can sometimes be the right move if we hit a Fermenter with it as well, but lockout is not a realistic goal. We will have trouble setting up a board. The only upside is that there generally is no Hermes and it feels so good when we can eke out a win in this matchup.

Combo Lines

I promised some of the most intricate lines in current Netrunner, so here are a couple of positions that came up in actual play. I've added the solution as separate image so you can try to find the lines yourself, if you'd like to.

Thank you for coming to my TED Talk.

decks.title: Hot Ones (9th @ Worlds 2026)
decks.author: sebastiank
decks.identity_zh: 玛格达琳·凯诺-切穆泰: 幕后建筑师
decks.description_html:
History

It is my pleasure to finally share what I have been working on since Vantage Point spoiler season. When Read-Write Share first saw the light of day, it struck me as being functionally similar to Bookmark, which was the lynchpin of a wild combo deck that former lead designer June Cuervo won 2017 US nats with (In terms of deckbuilding, being a netrunner boomer has its benefits). Immediately, like several other folks, I started theorycrafting Read-Write Share, and like a few other folks, I saw its potential in protecting Deep Dives from Running Hot damage. Exploration of this idea in the community seemed to stop after districts. It stopped for a good reason: the corp meta, at least for a while, was quite hostile- lots of stuff that either won before we were ready, sniped our running hots before we were ready, or otherwise made deep diving impossible. When I came back to playing netrunner in August before I locked in again to finish my master's thesis, I took my version of the deck to 2nd at NANPC Pittsburgh and 5th at a DC CTK. The surprise factor of the deck was great, however, the early continentals meta was still hostile, and the Pittsburgh players started bullying me with beatrice's Ob once they knew the matchup. My hope in Hot Ones being real had largely died by the time I came back to testing a week before I left for worlds. The addition of Joy Ride, which was a suggestion by Council that sped the deck up by about a turn, made me think it would be a cool deck to play at COS. As of Friday morning, I was pretty sure I was on KhusYUM for the main event because that deck has a lot of good matchups, granted more agency, and was a joy to play. Then, I went 4-1 with Hot Ones at COS. And I realized three things:

1) The dopamine hit of comboing out, as runner, in 2026, was freight train esque

2) Corps in the actual field were the most susceptible to BS at any point since VP's release

3) Playing my own decks and people complimenting me on them feels good

So I decided to go for it. It worked out well enough.

How to play/slots

In case it wasn't clear, this deck is trying to do something pretty messed up. We're trying to take an 8-10 click turn on turn 6 or 7 in which we sweep HQ with Cupellation and play 3 Deep Dives with clicks to spare. Typically, how you do this is draw a ton of cards while hosting Deep Dives on Read-Write Share, installing Simulchips and Stoneships, making some money, discarding icebreakers, and hoarding Running Hots in hand. Then, when you're ready (or when you're forced to), you do something like this (taken from my cut game vs Nervousnightjar):

Corp turn 7(?) He fast advances to 6 points, has winning Post-Trust Dividend in hand, ice on R&D and HQ, 7 credits

Runner turn (1 point and 18 cards left in deck): Pop Stoneship Chartroom, pop Stoneship Chartroom, play Running Hot, play Running Hot, , pop Read-Write Share, play Ritual to draw 7, hard install Gauss, play Joy Ride, he rezzes Unsmiling, let fire bc no Dives in hand yet, Simulchip in Cupellation, draw 5 cards including 2 Dives, steal going to 2 pts, run Archives, Cup something, run HQ, pop Cup, steal going to 3 pts, Simulchip back in Cupellation just in case I need it, Deep Dive going to 5 pts, Deep Dive going to 9 pts, gg.

To maximize chances, it's important to maintain flexibility- both in terms of the turn-by-turn and preparing for the combo itself. Early, I'd advise against going full spend-my-entire-turn-to-draw-10-cards mode, and save that for turn 4 or 5; you still need to reach a decent credit total and drawing into Running Hots too early will force you to discard good cards and make your next turn worse. Some games, it's going late and I haven't seen an RWS yet, so I just hold Deep Dives and hope Stoneship padding is enough to keep them safe. Other games, I haven't seen my Running Hots/Simulchips/breakers, so I have to draw the whole deck first. More and more though, I'm finding that playing a Ritual to draw 7 on the combo turn is both feasible and is good, so you don't usually need to draw the whole deck prior to the combo turn. Lastly on this front, while there are many times when you can combo, the question that you also need to ask is should you combo. If I don't go now, what are the chances that I'll get another turn? If I wait, will I have more clicks/have Cupellation ready? If I wait, will the Corp be able to make centrals too taxing?

We don't really make runs before the combo turn, especially if they involve breaking ice. This can be exploited by rushing quickly behind 1 ice, although you can jumpscare the corp sometimes by installing a breaker from hand and running.

Real but temporary breakers: This suite makes it possible to consistently combo when you approach the 15-20 credit mark. Other decks trying the combo during districts season played Nanuq, but good luck breaking ice cheaply with that. Revolver was scary to play in a meta that expected it and in a deck that gets hosed like no other if the corp tries to hate on you, but no killer comes close to its efficiency. Gauss > Propeller bc its just as efficient against a lot of stuff and its not worth getting hosed by a second ice type. Installing Gauss and Euler with simulchip on the combo turn is fantastic- for Revolver, the only effect is saving a credit on install and maintaining MU flexibility, so often I just hard install the gun.

Cupellation: Helps safeguard you against some bad Dive luck by giving you 3 extra accesses- 1 by snagging the top card of R&D, 2 from HQ. If you have cup access on the combo turn, I recommend first running R&D, then archives, then HQ: this way, if the top card of R&D is an agenda, you can still get something in archives to cup.

No Pelangi/Gachapon/additional breakers: Sometimes, you do run into the problem of not drawing into breakers early, so you have to combo a turn or two later. However, I decided spending slots to solve that problem, which is a relatively specific one, was not worth it.

No Pinhole/Airblades/Cybertrooper Talut: All of these have potential, but are harder to make use of then programs, which you can discard with relative abandon and reinstall with chip. In terms of tech, I have a "if it's only going to improve one matchup by 10%, it's not worth playing it" mindset. None of these cards seemed to improve the relevant matchups enough for it to be worth playing them over more money/draw. Talut is the one I'd have my eye on most going forward, especially if LEO picks up.

Hush: was the one tech card that crossed the threshold for me to consider it worth playing at this event, considering there is a lot of Weyland in the meta and their main counterplay to shenanigans is Event Horizon. At the bare minimum, having it in your heap is saving you credits/revolver counters if they pre-pop it and you don't preinstall it on the correct ice. At best, it is saving you a click AND all the resources it would take to run back. Ice these days has a lot of text so it almost always has a use- it's mostly a question of if that use is worth spending a chip on.

On the day

I went 6-2. I beat two Nuvems, a fast advance R+, a kill R+, a kill ED, and a fast advance Nebula. I lost to LEO 2x. In swiss, I genuinely tried pretending that I was just digging through my deck to find a key card that was at the bottom, but I don't think anyone believed me.

Should I play this deck?

If you live within a reasonable traveling distance of laura_42, no. Otherwise, potentially.

Stuff/shoutouts

This was my comeback to big tournament play after missing the entirety of 2026 districts, megacities, and continentals. I had initially planned to attend some of those, but needing to finish my master's degree in the midst of challenging personal stuff going on led me to not. This past summer, to be frank, sucked. I worked weeks of 14 hour days, barely got sleep, and lost most of my irl friends. Aspects of my mental health that may have been lying under the surface for years became stark and pervasive. My life will never be the same.

Overall, I'm really happy with how I did. However, after starting swiss 7-0, and after what I had gone through, I started to get the feeling that this might be my year. Maybe after all this, I would finally get the thing I had dreamed of most in the past 5 years: becoming Netrunner world champion.

However, if life has taught me anything, it's that it's impossible to predict the future. If competing in netrunner has taught me anything, it's that Worlds top cut is a great white shark tank populated by 15 other people who dream of winning worlds and the only way they can do that is by eliminating you. Every mistake leaves you liable to die a grisly death. I made my mistake against Augustus Caesar in Round 1 by not realizing that I could use Perfect Recall on every HQ access he took and win the game on my next turn. He found the 1-in-6. That put me on track to face Laura's LEO again in round 3. Then, it was over.

After I reached out my hand to Laura to concede, a lot of people patted me on the back, gave me hugs. For them I was thankful, but at the same time I just wanted to go somewhere where I could cry, which I hadn't done in a long time in response to a children's card game loss and definitely didn't want to do at 25 years old in front of a crowd. I found a nice spot on the other side of the fifth floor of the Palais de Congrès with fake plants and a good view of the city, and did a little sob. Looking out the windows on the Montréal skyline, it dawned on me for the first time, in sincerity, that I might never win worlds.

Winning worlds with my own decks would have been a fairy tale ending on a rough chapter of my life. However, life isn't even a book. It doesn't even have chapters. And even if I had won worlds, I still was going to come back home to have to deal with the same mental health problems and still have to figure out what I'm doing next in my life.

Sustained happiness has never come easy for me. It probably never will. If I'm honest with myself, winning worlds this year wouldn't have given me that. Heck, winning a continentals in the same city didn't. While my behavior is not always, or even often, reflective of this, deep down, I am of the mindset that life is less about what you accomplish and more about the character you show in the midst of challenges and how you treat others. And given the fact that I was able to even make it to Montréal this year and that people care enough about me to give me cups of bad coffee and let me regale them with my netrunner war stories at midnight in the middle of a parking lot outside of a closed game store while it may have also been raining, I might be doing okay on this front. However, there is definitely always room for improvement.

Now, that this is out there and I don't have to keep deleting and rewriting it, it is time for me to focus on "helping others" (rongydoge, 2026) and "touching grass" and other stuff that gets me out of my head and is also just generally good to focus on. In the end, my "Montréal defense" wasn't successful. Another defense was though, that of the thesis variety. If I'm honest with myself, that other defense was probably more consequential. And on second thought, it may have been a bit greedy to ask for two successful defenses in the same year, in addition to an Arsenal title win.

Huge thanks to everyone at NSG for putting on an outstanding tournament. Thanks to the Board/Meeting of Minds for lots of insightful practice in the leadup, to Harry, James, and Serj for being great roommates, and to all those people as well as pretty much everyone in TAI breakers, Diogene, rongydoge, and whiteblade for the laughs, encouragement, and hugs on the weekend.

Love y'all. Love this game. Always be running.

decks.title: 52 card pickup and other cultural experiences (16th @Worlds)
decks.author: OF15-15

decks.description_html:
When I missed Worlds last year, I really hoped I could pair '26 Worlds with a well-timed exchange semester or another "valid" reason to travel to Canada. Around the time worlds got announced, I got accepted for an exchange semester, but Norway wasn't really better than Germany for traveling purposes. Additionally, the semesters were overlapping and August and September were packed with university stuff. I realized I would probably not make Worlds again this year. I somehow managed to squeeze in two in-person districts and two in-person MCs and a bit of other board games, but as we got closer to Continentals season, my plans for EMEA disappeared and I moved two weeks earlier than anticipated. I was quite disappointed with the amount of Netrunner tournaments this year, especially since I hadn't played in any big online tournaments and had earned only around 6 beans in total. At some point, I started looking for plane tickets to Montréal, but right after I decided to go to worlds after all, the price more than doubled, so I took a step back and just set a reasonable price alarm for the flight.

Then I got sick, had to stay home for a week and started jamming on jnet. My shaper experiments were fun, but not particularly successful and I couldn't find an anarch deck I enjoyed playing. I'm usually a certified crim hater (ask @Tyrus about that), but I had some fun with Mercury before Elevation release, so I gave davz's Mercury a spin. I enjoyed the list and kept toying around with it, changing slots here and there. Maintenance Access and Reprise were both performing great, so they got more copies, while the RnD multiaccess wasn't very convincing and got reduced.

I enjoyed sticking transfers, but was too lazy to clear tags and people kept trashing my econ. That somehow made them feel less good and I swapped them out for the best econ card crim has. Now even less inclined to clear tags, my bypass didn't really work as intended. I cut the Nukas and replaced the Backstitchings with Crew. The only thing better than temporary bypass is permanent bypass, right?

At this point, the deck worked pretty well (to be fair, davz's list already worked great), but I didn't really have a tournament I could bring it to. I kept looking at the flights, and while the prices did vary a lot, they never got even close to the original one. After a lot of mental back and forth and some encouragement from other players to be more irresponsible with my money, I decided to book the flights. Luckily I first applied for the ETA, or at least tried to. Apparently, I left my passport in Germany, which is rather unfortunate for intercontinental travel.

But since the decision had been that hard, I was not ready to give up. It was already the Monday before worlds and I spent the better part of the evening searching for a feasible route instead of studying for my exam the next day. On Tuesday at 1am I decided to go with a plan with enough layover in Frankfurt to get the passport from my parents. Unfortunately, that meant I had to fly for the first time in my life, spend two nights at airports, drive 8 hours by train through Germany, enjoy a 9.5h layover in Ponta Delgada and leave for all of that within 16 hours.

And I went for it! It was a very exhausting trip, but surprisingly good! I got a few hours of free time with my parents, unexpectedly showed up at my old boardgame club's yearly tournament and had a lovely day in Ponta Delgada.

Luckily, there were still empty beds in some group booking at the hostel and I even got asked to join a CoS-Team. Both turned out to be way better than expected with my roommates being the king and Jai and my CoS-Team being the king and RustRyder. I packed some very nice Physarium alts and a Physarium token and it is a good card in general, so I decided to try out swapping an S-Dobrado for two Physariums and was surprisingly happy with it. I finally met @ManInTheMoon and at some point he mentioned playing a 49 card loup. The reasoning for it made sense and I realized that at least half of my runner losses in the last weeks were lockouts while ahead with both tempo and points. I remembered that playing more cards is a good counter to running out of deck, especially since the last 5-10 cards are class act cards anyway.

I always loved playing the same deck or partner decks with another person, and before I fell asleep, I saw a message from mitm that he went to 52. I decided to do the same. To keep the card ratios intact I looked for some good event money, but all of the influence-free cards were already used. I managed to free three pips by playing more copies of WAKE and Lie Low instead of their influence-costing version. Already deep in the meme-territory, I went for 3x Wildcat Strike and double Tread Lightly.

When I woke up, I was still convinced by my own reasoning (and my 1am decisions worked out for the flights), but it seemed bad in so many ways. I got some emergency consulting from @Tyrus and he told me that my reasoning was in fact valid, so I submitted the list and grabbed some last-minute proxies.

Same as in testing, the deck was a ton of fun during the tournament. My corp was more on the boring side, but Mercury was on fire and pulled some very sick lines. My favourite was probably against @Huckleberry Finn, where I stole something first click, played a Reprise to bounce a Maskirovka and force a Biawak rez, played a second Reprise to bounce the Biawak and finished off with Transferring to 2 credits. As far as I could tell, my opponents had fun as well and I definitely had some really really good games of Netrunner. After 14 tense, but fun rounds, I ended up in 16th place, just barely making the cut. There I had to corp twice, which did not end well.

While I originally planned to go hiking in Canada after worlds (that's why I walked around in those very light hiking shoes all the time btw), I got invited to join a larger group going to Toronto. Since I thought that would still leave me with enough time afterwards, I happily joined. A trip to CostCo and a lot of Fast Food were definitely a cultural experience, although I'll be happy to have my European food back soon.

After visiting the Niagara falls a day later, ManInTheMoon and Ariel talked me into joining them on a trip to the US, so I ended up going to Buffalo and then Philadelphia. I planned my way back with a two day stop in NYC for sightseeing, a Broadway Show (more culture 🎉) and some Netrunner games. Everything went according to plan until I tried to go back into Canada and the border officer told me that my flight out of Montreal was not later the same day, but the day after. After some back and forth, I was allowed to travel into Canada, found someone to host me for the night and even got to go for an extended walk on a large hill near Montreal. The hiking shoes were finally vindicated.

some card choices

Crew

Crew provides a permanent answer to the most annoying ice you're facing: This includes cheap gearchecks like Ping, Tatu-Bola, Descent, and Afshar which do something useful for the corp while still being as hard to bypass as Drafter or Maskirovka. VSA is no gearcheck and doesn't keep you out, Crew is the only way to deal with it at all. Event Horizon is obviously the best target against weyland. With most our tools being single use, well-placed Event Horizons can take away multiple accesses at once. Interesting Targets are Sleipnir, Tree Line and Winchester. Placed on HQ, they make early transfers very hard and if you can find both crews, this is always a good surprise. This list doesn't care about tags most of the time, so that's not really a downside.

Lie Low

In a rich, large deck, this is simply doing a decent job at drawing you cards (roughly the same as Steelskin on play actually). It's even more useful against Oppo or Behold, where it is always nice to fully clear Oppo or Behold from low credits. Also helps in case you need to detag after tagging yourself.

Wildcat Strike

A Gamble that can be played from 2 credits. Terms and Conditions apply. Sometimes people misplay and give you cards. Never blank since you don't run out of deck.

Reprise

Snowballs you from points 3 and 4 to point 7.

Maintenance Access

Basically a Hermes/Reprise Trigger on demand if HQ is locked.

WOKE Implant v2A-JRJ

decks.description_html:
I won't let my friends hear the end of the fact that I was the highest placed Earth Station in the world at the ̶E̶d̶i̶n̶b̶u̶r̶g̶h̶ ̶2̶0̶2̶5̶ Montreal 2026 World Championships :D

As I realized I had played maybe 10 games of Netrunner in the 6 months leading up to worlds, I began to get scared that I wouldn't have the wherewithal to defend my title as the world's best Earth SEA. How would I know what I'd be up against? Turns out, if you believe in the heart of the cards, it truly doesn't matter.

This is largely just a copy of my last year's deck, with a few minor updates.

Things of note:

  • Flagship: I really thought, when this card released, that I would love using it and would appreciate it a lot more than I do. Turns out, it's a little cheap to trash when compared to its ancestor, and honestly, didn't even feel required. I had a few games where I was flipped the large majority of the game, and one game in particular where I never flipped back. Sick.
  • Event Horizon: Part of why Flagship wasn't required was because this card has great text. Nothing notable beyond calling out that it fills the need that Flagship would otherwise fill.
  • Sacrifice Zone Expansion: This card has been yapped about in many other circles, but in Earth SEA, it is an incredible card. The defense you're able to put up allowed me to get multiple 3-credit gains before scoring it and jamming another one right down. Amazing as both econ as well as points.
  • Digital Rights Management: This little baby is used to grab the above when you need econ + a push. As expected, and as the same as last year, didn't see this bad boy come up a single time over the tournament. Typical 1-of.
  • Predictive Planogram: Hitting a Seb with Predictive 'Rashida Jaheem mode' as he floated a tag felt good. Usually, this is for if runners assume I have no tag 'punishment', as it lets me propel my game further, but it also oftentimes helps me recover if the runner forced an expensive rez too early, as the 0->3c swing can be very nice.
  • Transport Monopoly: Card sucks
  • Seamless Launch vs The Holo Man: Holo is fun, I was toying with a clown-car bad pub HQ Earth Sea with Flagship and The Red Room and Shackleton Grid, but boy is that all expensive for a single remote to build money for! Therefore, we just rely on Seamless Launch and The Basalt Spire to score out. Straightforward. I will revisit this fun idea of a clown car Earth SEA in the very future, so get ready for that hullabaloo, if you've bothered to read this far.
  • Earth Station: SEA Headquarters: The amount of times a runner had to re-read this ID makes it worth playing alone. In probably 4 out of my 6 games, the runner had to re-read it at least once during the match.

I only wanted and prayed to get a single win as Earth SEA this Worlds tournament, so I am stoked with how well this deck performed. I got scared for my place when I saw that the Earth SEA players increased by a whopping 50% when I arrived to the tournament (a whole 3 people!!), but the best Earth SEA managed to stay on top. Haha. I jest.

All in all, I had a great time this year at Worlds, and loved visiting a new city and meeting new folks! Already excited for next year.

I play Startup once per year, at Worlds, and always have a lovely time of it. Constrained deckbuilding is fun, and figuring out the best decks possible from a limited pool is a puzzle I enjoy. Startup emphasizes Netrunner fundamentals in a pronounced way, and I dig that.

A couple days before leaving for Worlds, I had made Melies U and Flood PD Startup decks online, but then noticed R+ had just been unbanned earlier that week and was legal for Worlds. I poked around to see what cards might make it viable, and quickly fell into this all-red, Jinteki blood festival that wildly pairs with the plentiful R+ tagging package here.

The spectre of Unleash + Vicsek has been haunting the edges of the competitive Standard meta all year, and this leans fully into that plan as a kill backup, but scoring is real here too with Flood the Market and 3/2s and 4/2s, the board for which can be established fairly quickly. I momentarily considered playing this in Standard, with some tweaks, since it was my creation, but having zero reps or doing any stress testing with it seemed ill-advised. I might make this a post-Worlds pet project.

The worst part of playing Startup at Worlds is it means you missed the Top 16 cut, and in my case, was one game off from making it in, the past two years in a row. That’s a bitter pill, but getting to play in another Netrunner tournament immediately after the swallow really helps me move on from the disappointment. I’ve historically had good runs at these tournaments, so they’re a nice way to wrap Worlds. This year, there was a four-way tie for first place, with 5-1 records and no cut, so I landed 3rd on SOS. decks.title: Graphic Design is My Prison (3rd @ PH Costume Party)
decks.author: lunari
decks.identity_zh: 网际传媒：掌控讯息
decks.description_html:
3rd @ Costume Party after iterating on this and a bunch of other decks for the tournament. Pretty silly given it was just a GNK but you know, might as well since there's some new (old) IDs.

I wanted to go through some changes I made while building the deck to somehow give budding deckbuilders some perspective on how to build decks for specific formats.

The Decks I Tried

We tested out a bunch of decks for Costume Party and I'll list down some of them.

  • Titan Transnational: Investing In Your Future + Remastered Edition: I wanted to play Astrotrain, but the deck just couldn't generate enough credits before runners could set up. And after you Big Deal, the Runners can just race you to points. Very soft to Transfer of Wealth too.

  • Haas-Bioroid: Precision Design Slash and Burn Agriculture: Install + Advance + Slash and Burn Agriculture a 3/2, then recur Slab to HQ was fun in concept, but again, you just kinda lose to the Reg Runner decks. Tranquility Home Grid was crucial in this type of jamming deck, since you only really need 2 credits to score out, but this gets eaten alive by Whizzard: Master Gamer.

  • Haarpsichord Studios: Entertainment Unleashed + Let Them Dream + Megaprix Qualifier: Asset spam and just outrace the Runner, specially when you also have Nightmare Archive. You can also form a kill fork with Distributed Tracing + Hypoxia. This loses to Whizzard: Master Gamer and Heartbeat.

  • Cybernetics Division: Humanity Upgraded + ZATO City Grid + Bumi 1.0. Land one core damage. Afterwards, you can threaten a Measured Response or Distributed Tracing + End of the Line kill. Loses if the Runner never touches the remote. Also Heartbeat.

  • Ob Superheavy Logistics: Extract. Export. Excel. + Saisentan + Hafrún: As suggested by Council. Definitely fun, but Heartbeat is a problem.

  • NBN: Controlling the Message + Aggressive Trendsetting and other 1-pointers. Still felt slow. If the Runner builds up, you're not really threatening anything fast enough to outscale. If you plan to play it with a kill fork, you're also being threatened by Heartbeat and Apocalypse.

The Decks I Didn't Try

  • Cerebral Imaging: Infinite Frontiers is probably good and CyberspacePanda was planning on bringing it, but I didn't want to play CI. YDL for piles of cash must feel good lol

  • Editorial Division: Ad Nihilum but Green: Felt so creatively bankrupt; the deck almost builds itself so I didn't wanna look into it. Definitely has teeth, though! Easy pick as a great deck to build and play at your event.

  • Argus Security: Protection Guaranteed. Same as above.

Good Runner Decks

Before I talk about the iterations, I also want to outline what I feel like are the strongest decks in the meta:

  • Crim Whizzard: Master Gamer: you have value vs everything. Even remoteless decks have trashables.

  • Crim Sunny Lebeau: Security Specialist: DreamNet and 25 influence? You can play everything, 3 Nuka, Airblades, Leech, Steelskin, Hannah.

  • Anarch Kabonesa Wu: Netspace Thrillseeker: Just pump your Rising Tide to beat fair decks, on-demand Gourmand for unfair decks and an Easy Mark on demand is great.

The Deck

People ask "What's was this deck originally?" Nothing. This wasn't originally an AU Co. deck, this was built from the ground up instead of taking an existing deck and just swapping out the ID.

So after getting whooped by Whizzard or Heartbeat a whole lot no matter what I tried, I wanted to build a non-CI deck that tries to: 1) have some equity vs Whizzard, and 2) can outgrind Apex: Invasive Predator.

NBN: Controlling the Message was the one ID I felt like could have some fighting chance vs Whizz if I decided to play an asset deck, and grinding out Apex was what led me to inflating my deck size to 64.

Phase 1 The initial list was only 54 cards and played fewer Regenesis, no The Powers That Be and ran End of the Line + Gaslight to score quick kills. It also had some Urtica Cipher and See How They Run for more kill forks. I had like 5 ice in the deck. I realized this was just terrible the moment Heartbeat got dropped in front of me lol

Phase 2 I kept the EotL line, but added more assets and Byte!, and more ice to keep Apex out of the servers, or at least make it more painful / taxing. But Eotl still wasn't cutting it.

Phase 3 I dropped the EotL line completely and started looking for better influence spends. Since I was adding more cards to the deck, I shifted influence to Let Them Dream to satisfy agenda requirements, but also so I don't have to draw too many points all at once. It was also better for Moon Pool and actually gave the deck better score out lines so I don't feel to pressured tossing out the LtDs to archives. This was also the time I started moving away from See How They Run and into Orbital Superiority. Still loses to most decks.

Phase 4 I waved the flag, took out the cheeky kill cards and just added actual ice like Attini and Boto to tax the runner out. I needed more money though, so I made space for Hansei Review and Charlotte Caçador as well.

Phase 5 Now that I had some money, I actually had to figure out what to do with the tags. With End of the Line out, what can I use the tags for? Unleash Cloud Eater was in faction and played well with what the deck has now shaped into, so I tried it out. If we're grinding out the Runner, the Unleash on a Cloud Eater could flatline, or just trash any card. This also led to Retribution: since we were doing spiky things, we could also trash breakers to lock runners out eventually with even just Tatu-Bola. This has happened more than once, so it felt like a good include.

Phase 6 I need more moneyyyy I need to be fasterrrrr!!! What if the Runner sits back a little and builds before contesting? What happens if they have money (or link) to beat the trace and detag a big Oppo Research after? I had to accelerate a little bit via La Costa Grid, so I could get Charlotte money faster, or just score agendas faster to build up Phật Gioan Baotixita pings. I also then dropped a Sericulture Expansion for 2x Hybrid Release and the last inf was spent on a The Powers That Be for more acceleration. This was also when I went to 3x Front Company and it has become the deck's cornerstone.

The Gameplan

Ideally you want to start spamming agendas as early as turn 1. Most decks in the format set up on turn 1 (DreamNet, Apex install, Kabonessa tutor, Geist bs), so you're going to get value out of it.

You want to keep the threat of Oppo Research always live, so you need to present forks such as: rezing Phat when you know they need to set up/are recovering after a trash + detag, presenting La Costa + Charlotte when they're building up, scoring a Regenesis to remind them you can actually score out, so they have to run somewhere.

You eventually want to ice up HQ and R&D with Attini, Cloud Eater, or Boto. Once both centrals are iced up, you then rez the Front Company and not anytime before that. You want the Front Company to stick by making the run to trash it extremely painful.

From there, you can build a sort of prison where it's going to hurt to run anywhere on centrals, then they have to take care of assets not named Front Company, then you threaten with an Oppo Research afterwards.

A tip when playing the deck: you don't need to rez your assets asap. Keep them guessing until you present the pseudo-prison. Rezzing both Front Company and Phat on the same turn is a complex boardstate for the Runner to solve.

Deck Changes

Looking back, I would definitely run 3x Bladderwort: it's not Bio-Ethics Association, but it can do an approximation of the job sometimes when you're rezzing expensive ice, La Costa Grid, or Moon Pool just to duck credits. The Byte! can definitely go. I would also consider Hostile Architecture, but that would also eat up the influence.

Main Takeaways

When building Corp decks, I always have questions to ask myself:

How does this deck win? This is what starts your deck off. Maybe you just want to Seamless Launch agendas. Maybe you want to End of the Line them. Maybe you want to Unleash a Tyr or a Cloud Eater. Start building from here.

Is it through flatline? If so, what are you doing to make them spend credits so you can Measured Response them? How are the tags sticking so you can End of the Line them?

If scoring, how are you keeping the Runner from accessing your agendas? Some hide them among assets, some just have very expensive servers, some play the never-advance game.

If the Runner trashes your cards, how are you going to recover? Usually it's the Oppo Research punish. Sometimes it's Measured Response.

This is more for the kill decks: if the Runner does nothing, how do you win? Hyperbolically speaking, if the Runner clicks for 4 credits every turn and does nothing else, can your deck win? The R+ kill deck at worlds forces interaction via Reaper Function and Orbital Superiority.

But also, if you're a scoring/asset deck, can you win fast enough if the Runner builds up before contesting all your assets/servers? The Combo PD deck does this well and can win really fast, since it's asking for three different breakers every time you want to check a new remote early, plus a constant stream of credits.

The above examples are massive oversimplifications of Netrunner, but I think still gets the point across: you have to be able to win whether Runner acts or not.

I'm still learning how to deckbuild and I have had a lot of help figuring out how to build decks along the way from players way better and more experienced than me. This deck was a blast to build, iterate on, and play!

These are just some tips, but I hope this helped out those who want to try building their own decks in the future, regardless of the format!

decks.author: laura_42
