decks.description_html:
...along the way.

A few days ago, I had a dream that I made top 50 at my first worlds. I was really happy that I had done so well, and then I woke up and remembered I actually made it to the top 10. I still can’t believe this happened. How did we get here?

Step 1: Burn out (slightly).

Cascadia was a blast. I was so proud that Twink Shipping, the first joint effort between Lia, Cybershark, and I performed so well, and quickly became yet another SCRUBS meta menace. It’s always a pleasure to see how quickly the Netrunner community picks up decks and adapts them to pose new problems to the runner or adapt to personal play style.

But I was becoming aware of how our beloved Phật Ob could be beaten by aggressive, Criminal economic pressure. Cards like Cup and Bahia Bands were also being slotted as tech to stop us from the tempo crimes of Svyatogor. I hated finding myself in an endgame where all my assets were trashed and I just had to hope for the runner to trip into Measured Response or miss my fast advance pieces in hand. With reg Vic no longer scared off by the big red university, runners seemed to be able to accrue so much late-game value that they could trample over corporations.

Step 2: Watch from the sidelines.

At this point, I should just own up to my reputation as a jnet spectator. If you’ve heard a ping in your jnet lobby between the hours of 12 PM - 3 AM EST, there’s good odds it’s me. But I’d genuinely recommend it; I’ve learned so much from watching games closely. You can see interesting deckbuilding choices others are making, you can see the consequences of someone taking plays that you didn’t, you can practice processing the unknown information on board states. I continued having a blast volunteering to do commentary – shoutout to NSG and maninthemoon’s online showdowns for lots of opportunities to do so! – as I'm really just talking on top of my usual jnet spectating.

Unfortunately, what I witnessed was not really helping my general reticence towards the meta. If corporations couldn’t outlast Vic in the late game, the other option was to outrush them. The development of another SCRUBS meta menace “funnty r+” and the re-emergence of flood PD weren’t really styles of play that interested me (setting aside by brief flirtation with combo PD). Not to mention, the prevalence of these decks in the meta would have been an absolute nightmare for me to continue playing my beloved, best faction of shaper. What was I to do? Despair and give in to the call of spikiness, telling me to just play reg Vic and R+...?

Step 3: Play Slay the Spire 2.

If I was feeling burned out on Netrunner, I figured I should listen to my body. I recalled tuno’s bit of advice that “Brains stop learning if you continuously tire them over a monotonous routine where you always do the same thing. “Grinding” is often a terrible idea. Every once in a while, stop playing Netrunner for a while.” So I had more important things to do than refine a tier 0 deck: hang out with Lia and Melody after our too brief time together in Cascadia, let them get me into StS2 after my long-standing insistence that I prefer board games to video games, teach them Spirit Island and Sakura Arms in return. I would love to pretend that StS2 taught me some secret calculating techniques that I used to do well at worlds. But really what I learned is that I didn’t have to stress about worlds. No matter how many games I won or lost, I would get to spend time with some of my favourite people, guaranteed. What more could I want?

So I decided that I would go to worlds playing something I found fun, something that felt like me. On the runner side, after some conversations with Minstrel, we found ourselves circling back to DeeR’s Magdalene all the way from early Elevation meta. DeeR’s deck has a special place in my heart after propelling me to 2nd at my first big event of Vancouver Megacities. So if I was playing my runner from Vancouver, I thought, why not my corp…

Step 4: Go to a CTK.

Leading up to worlds, rohit organized a CTK for the NYC area. Rohit had been playing metrixgo’s Boto LEO at locals for some time, and while it was a bit weak to criminal pressure like I’d expected, I was quite impressed with it. The ice was taxing, LEO still made run events hard to land, and good lord that agenda suite was miserable to steal. But I was suspicious about the choice of Boto. If Criminal was our worst matchup, doesn’t that just provide baby-Brans for Curupira to farm in the early game?

What were the other options? HB’s taxing code gates don’t go beyond 4 strength, so overindexing on them is asking to get run over by Tungsten Tailor Buzzsaw. Hence the only remaining option: welcome to sentry hell. Bumi and Drafter are famously already a problem for Carmen (without any strength support like Leech). “But what about Revolver?” you ask, clever reader. Yes, Revolver is a pretty fucked up killer. But it only has so many bullets, and as soon as the gun is empty, that means the runner has to stop interacting and go find their next killer, buying you turns to econ-up and score.

I went back to my favourite pieces of pet ice: Týr, Ansel 1.0 , and Ansel 2.0. I looked at the ice, thought “hey these are pretty expensive,” and remembered that Nuvem has been cheating out big ice for free recently. Enter: Reanimation Protocol. Would this card rot in hand early game? Probably. Would the bad pub catch up to me? Who knows. But in the spirit of whimsy and experimentation, I sleeved up this deck idea, with 1 of each big sentry to test which one I’d like the most on the day, and took it to the CTK.

After going 2-1 against Criminals, including a game where I got transferred to 0 two turns in a row, I started to believe the deck might be real. I continued to take this deck to locals and had a blast remembering how LEO can build to such powerful lockouts, not to mention the highs and lows of ADT either ripping a free Týr or showing no installables. Locals were all the testing I really needed, considering the caliber of the NYC meta.

At this point in the writeup, I have to shout out the folks who play in NYC. Despite my [number redacted] too many games on jnet, the players here have truly shaped me into the player I am now. It was my honour repping the NYC playmat on stream. Playing my earliest games into kysra, rohit, Radiant, xdg, coldlava, wyld, and Dave976 was the best training I could have asked for. Getting better at the game alongside Wynaut and floatingfast was an absolute treasure. And most important of all: thank you chia for being the best TO, stream organizer, and friend I could ask for.

Step 5: Play at worlds I guess!

The only changes I made from my CTK list were -1 Hansei for +1 Planogram, to help those aforementioned Transferred-to-0 turns, -1 Petty Cash for +1 M.I.C. after a game where I drew no ice, and -1 Manegarm for +1 Scapenet. Manegarm was usually overkill in the remote, and I noticed that Vics were doing more runs for DreamNet value so Scapenet would be online more often.

The deck went 4-1 at CoS and 6-2 in the main event. Some highlights:

CoS Round 3 against rustryder’s Seb: I rez a Sleipnir. He contemplates whether he can afford to spend a Charm to Crew it. He leans over to The King and asks, “So what’s my gameplan against LEO?” who responds, “I don’t know, touch agendas?” After locking out the runner pretty convincingly, I learn that this deck has a really good Seb matchup by using the LEO ability to end Transfers and Privileged Accesses, and holding onto Reanimation to bring back ice after they destroy it.

CoS Round 4 against not_yeti’s Vic: He hesitantly keeps his hand, so I jam Bumi on HQ and HR + Sleipnir in remote. He sends a Transfer, so I trade the Bumi, and then he trashes HR and draws. I look at the Regolith I have in hand and ask out loud, “What are the odds you’ve drawn your second Transfer already?” before installing the Regolith and clicking it twice. He transfers me again. Somehow I still manage to claw back this game by putting the sentry hell plan into action, taxing out Revolver bullets and getting way more Drafter fires than I’ve ever hoped for in my life.

Swiss Round 5 against iss44ru’s Vic: He’s playing well but hasn’t drawn quite enough money. He’s run with Cezve to start charging his Twinning. I look at his token pool: 6 credits. I think to myself, “Scapenet would be an amazing draw here.” I swear I heard the heavens open when I saw my mandatory draw.

Swiss Round 9 against sebk’s Running Hot Maggie: I’d just seen sebk beat my teammate (and friend and future king of swiss) @jxue16 so I knew just how explosive this runner could be. I plan to ice up centrals and use the LEO ability to tax his credits and clicks on the big combo turn. Instead, I draw barely any ice and a bunch of trains. I figure that he probably wants to save his temporary breakers for the combo turn, so I form a new plan: jam out of the remote like a bad PD impression and hope his dives whiff. Before I know it, he’s sending the combo. First Running Hot, snipes a Deep Dive. Second and third Running Hot. He has more clicks than I know what to do with. He does a big Ritual to draw up. He rips the first Deep Dive: nothing. He rips the second Deep Dive: one Let them Dream. I let out a sigh of relief and jam my trains out of the remote now that he’s burned through his resources.

Swiss Round 10 against Minstrel on Khusyuk Maggie: I’m looking forward to this matchup since back when I played Khusyuk, LEO was an absolute nightmare matchup as the ID ability could end your Khusyuk run after breaking all the ice. I keep a greedy (iceless) hand since it has a Humanoid, but I draw into enough agendas that I need to ice HQ in case of Burner. I’m still not drawing any ice, but I make a read that he’s still setting up his board, letting me sneak out a Tranq Grid-looking Humanoid on the table. I flood so bad that I pitch a Send a Message, telling myself “if I’ve made one big bluff this game already, why not another?” You can watch the whole game on stream! (In hindsight, I should have taken this game much slower. Rather than trying to outrush shaper like usual, glaciering and setting up the LEO ability makes the runner deck’s game plan of Khusyuk and Burner pretty miserable.)

Cut Round 3 rematch against sebK: This was my favourite corp game of worlds. (Even though it was a bit of a blowout, sorry seb, I know you’d hoped to dodge my LEO in the cut.) I’d rather not just cross my fingers and brace the Deep Dives again, so this time I glacier up on centrals. I score an early ADT which gets a free Týr onto R&D. SebK does manage to grab a Let them Dream from the remote and one from HQ as he attempts the combo turn, but the combination of Tyr and Bran on R&D is too expensive and he has to give up on diving. With 15-20 minutes left, the score is tied 2-2. I ask the judge, “who’s the higher seed?” It’s him. We then spend the next 5 minutes clicking for credits at a breakneck pace, as I’m waiting to draw Seamlesses and agendas. I bait out a run on a remote Humanoid, so I Scapenet threatening his last Simulchip. I pay all my money into a trace 19(!), he pays all of his money to protect it. We click for credits some more. With 5 minutes ticking down, I jam and score a Train, and then a SAM to close the game. He simply doesn’t have enough bullets to get through the remote of Bumi, Bumi, and Ansel 2.0. (This game also marked the second time I got a player to ask a judge for the text on Ansel 2.0.)

Cut Round 4 against davz’s big Maggie: You can also watch this game on stream! I frankly wasn’t expecting this much Shaper in the top cut, so I didn’t have much experience with the matchup. From having played the runner side, I remember finding it annoying when the corp rushes to game point while I’m still setting up, since there ends up being a constant never-advance threat with Seamless. I draw enough early Seamlesses and ice that I can score out a train (after he ran it last click, which really made me twirl my fictional diabolical moustache). Soon after, I jam a Let them Dream. He’s a bit poor and debating whether to run, so he asks me, “Would you mind telling me what that is?” I chuckle and reply, “No it’s face-down, that’s my favourite part of the game.”

He lets me have the Dream, so the plan to rush to game point is in action. But on that same turn, I topdeck a train into hand. I have a choice when I score Let them Dream: do I bottom the train, or do I bottom the Send a Message in R&D (which is the most vulnerable to Deep Dive)? I tell myself that it’s safe in hand as only a 1 in 5, so I bottom the SAM and play it cool. That was my biggest mistake, as I learn that one of Davz’s skills is ripping sick 1-in-5s out of hand. But my whole tournament run already felt like such a dream on borrowed time, I absolutely cannot be upset about going out to a player of the caliber of davz.

Step 6: Celebrate!

Worlds was an absolute pleasure. It was great getting to meet the players who I’d known online (Davz, Minstrel, Jai, notyeti, AugustusCaesar, nervousnightjar, dull_bulb). The energy of a room full of people watching the top cut games in bated breath was electrifying. And the diversity of decks I saw in the top cut has reinvigorated my excitement for Netrunner again! On the same day I got back from my flight, I booted up jnet and just *had* to give the KhusYUM deck a go. So, I’m not sure if the moral of my story is that the way to deal with burnout is to play less Netrunner or to play more Netrunner. Both, I guess? Really it’s this: play games with people that you love and you will love those games.

Some of those people:

  • Thank you to SCRUBS members, present and past: Fabio, anarchomushroom, Lap, ChonkySeal, Tang, NotAgain, Stwyde, protheseus, 34Witches, and jonny. You were the first testing group that took me in and fostered my original LEO arc. It’s always a joy to play against y’all, you obsessive, incredible, hilarious netrunners. Extra shoutout to Stwyde for gifting me the acrylic LEO that I played all weekend. At this point, I assume it must be blessed with magic luck.

  • My love to QtM: frogs, izzy, Trillian, ivy, squeeeeeege, Harp, picat, chia (again), and more. You showed me how a community forms around this beautiful game, and without you I would have burned out far earlier.

  • The Vancouver meta: Sindarin, Solomir, aruzan, Friday, GhostMeat, hams, Sokka, Whiteblade, keith, Kamran. My huge gratitude to Sindarin's TO work, as I’ve somehow had my best results at your events, and I was able to do well at Worlds by recreating that hometown magic (by bringing versions of my first megacity decks). I’m so glad I got to get to show off the Science World Let them Dreams on stream, and I'm still treasuring those foil Measured Responses with my life!

  • The NYC meta, I already shouted you out before but you’re so awesome you get another shoutout.

  • CyberShark, I’m always learning new things from you and your micro-optimizations and esoteric rules knowledge. You’re a far better runner than you give yourself credit for, testing against you is worth a dozen other games. And your undefeated* Ob streak is outrageously impressive. You’re the cornerstone that helps hold our whole group together.

  • Melody, thank you for being my rock. I don’t know how you made my nerves magically disappear all weekend; your hugs are the real secret tech. I'm so grateful I met you through this game and I'm so excited to keep going to more events together. I really couldn’t have done it without you. All my wins are yours too.

  • Lia. My commentary/streaming partner in crime, my spreadsheet maker, my Knickknack-killer, and the greatest Criminal player I’ve ever witnessed. From the very first time we met (I think I was info-dumping about how to play as and against LEO then too) it was obvious that the way you thought about Netrunner is a viewpoint I needed in my life. Your perspective has blended with mine so much at this point that I could never pull apart the countless ways you’ve affected me. Your friendship has been a joy and a gift.

My love to you all.

(Oh yeah how do you play this deck? More or less typical LEO stuff: keep Mercia safe, ice up centrals to deny run value (especially an ice on Archives against Pinhole and DreamNet), install an asset + upgrade together to disincentivize Pinholing, try to save Seamlesses for the 5/3, Let them Dream can bottom agendas or fetch an agenda to hand to jam next turn. Playing with Reanimation can be a bit unintuitive: pitch some ice to Hansei or overdrawing to set it up, anticipate the runner's end-game rig and decide which ice will be the most taxing, hold off on Reanimating if you expect ice destruction, don’t Reanimate too early against Criminal or the bad pub will add up. And in general, the trick with LEO is simply to shut down all the runner’s outs. Hope you have fun with the deck! LEO is real!!)

decks.title: butts in seats (Worlds 2026 winner)
decks.author: Crunchums
decks.identity_zh: 哈斯生化: 精密设计
decks.description_html:
Links: ABR, Cobra, The Maker's Eye

-

A claim in this Athlici writeup caught my eye:

My median corp game in conts was won in 7.5 turns and saw 5 fully ops played. What can I say, deck is still good 🤷‍♂️. Even with my opponents playing very well it generally felt more like my game to lose...

It sounds too good to be true, but I play two jnet casual games and easily win on turn 7 and on turn 8 despite not really knowing what I’m doing. Hey, Flood PD seems kinda messed up! Other Snarebears also mess around with the archetype and reach the same conclusion.

Then for a few weeks the Snarebears become obsessed with butts. Jonas (tbu3k) posts a build with 15 assets and 14 ice that includes 3 Nanoetching Matrix, 2 Tiered Subscription (props to Kikai for Tiered Flud; 3x Tiered Subscription is brilliant), and 3 Reverb, and we iterate on it. The thought is (borrowing terms from another Athlici writeup): what if we stopped trying to rush and went full attrition? We’re playing so many 3-4 butt cards that you’re often able to out-butt Loup and Seb!

But However there are doubts. Aren’t we giving up a lot by not playing acceleration? The “slow” version spends its turns clicking to install and clicking to draw until it finds Flop; the “fast” version gets to zoom ahead with Humanoid Resources and Predictive Planogram. Eventually we conclude: yeah butts are great, and the psychic damage you deal when the runner runs an installed Nanoetching Matrix or Calvin B4L3Y is exquisite, but firing HR is really really good. Out with some butts, in with 2 HR 2 PP.

So was the butt-journey all for nothing? No: it taught us about the value of seats. The popular lists were playing 9-11 ice whereas this build is playing 13. By dropping operations like Corporate Hospitality and Greasing the Palm for more ice, you’re giving up some of your high-roll capability in exchange for bricking less often on not drawing enough ice (Flop and Flood need butts and seats), more flexibility with icing centrals, and bigger Flops on average.

We also learned the power of playing the deck in a more reg style as opposed to aiming for one-turn combos. Any time you can score an agenda while staying economically liquid you probably should: every agenda you score is an agenda the runner can no longer steal, and PD-ing back a Flop accelerates you forward.

-

Eight Snarebears played this exact list to a combined record of 45-12:

  • Max (Crunchums) 10-0 1st
  • Jon (Janktivist) 8-1 4th
  • Dan (cableCarnage) 4-3 10th
  • Chris (analyzechris) 7-0
  • Dee (DeeR) 5-2
  • Kyle (Aureates) 4-2
  • Ben (Safer) 3-2
  • Ian (rongydoge) 4-2*

*reported as 3-3 (in round 10 he played a game and won but then conceded when he realized his opponent had been paired down)

breaking down those 12 losses:

  • 3 were to fellow Snarebears (Max on MuslihaT, Dave (Ghost Meat) on Zahya, Jon on Loup)
  • 4 were to Seb (2x jxue16, 2x 34Witches)
  • 5 were to non-bears who weren't on Seb (not_yeti on Vic, trebiushawke on Esâ, Slapdash on Arissana, emaaaly on Zahya, Redino987 on MuslihaT)

-

Is Flood PD broken? Does some part of it need to be banned?

The deck definitely has bad matchups. Seb is a nightmare (Audrey, Transfer of Wealth, Gourmand, Wheels, Crew). Zahya has a ton of multiaccess, gets paid for taking accesses, and can snipe your operations with Cupellation. Loup is scary when he’s on Audrey, and is still capable of giving you trouble when he isn't.

(I was fortunate to dodge all of those matchups: I played against 6 Vic, 3 Mags, and 1 Esâ.)

I also think runners can do better into the deck by running remotes more aggressively:

  • The deck is going to table some agendas in most games because 1) having a pre-installed agenda makes it easier to pull off combos 2) sometimes they’re the only butts you have available 3) tabling agendas is often safer than keeping them in HQ (especially if the runner isn’t running remotes)
  • The only scary facecheck is Drafter, and it’s only really bad to hit if it’s getting back Flop or an HR that’s going to fire
  • The deck is actually quite poor before it goes crazy with Flop (the only other money cards are 2 HR, 2 PP (which it prefers to use for draw), and 2 Tiered) and really doesn’t want to spend credits rezzing ice

So as long as you’re not risking a bad Drafter fire you can hunt for table agendas (and HR) and trash some of their butts while you’re at it (which in addition to taking away combo pieces also makes it more likely that they will need to table agendas). If they rez ice that puts them further away from comboing and also maybe means there’s an agenda in that server. It helps if you have some sort of drip going so that you can afford to trash the unrezzed (non Wage Workers) butts that you see.

You can see this strategy in action in my streamed game running against Jon. It doesn’t flip the matchup or anything (this was actually our third time playing this exact matchup in the tournament; he won the previous two games and definitely could have won this one too if he drew more Flops), but as the corp it feels more challenging to play against than the runner just pounding away at centrals. Flop is a messed up card, but the real power of the deck lies in the fact that you have 6 agendas in 44 cards and the runner needs to touch 3 of them. If you can’t win by kicking the butts out of the seats (e.g. with Seb, Loup, or Azimat) then the most important thing is to be trying to suss out where the agendas are (HQ, R&D, archives, table) and adjusting your play accordingly.

Additional arguments against banning anything:

  • A new set is coming out in January, which might give runners new tools that are good against the deck
  • The current meta is pretty great (at least in my opinion)
  • Banning something would take away some of the fun of letting the meta evolve based on what we saw at worlds

All of that said I think it would be totally reasonable to ban Fully Operational. It does clearly messed-up things, and the dynamic of Flood PD games being heavily determined by how many Flops the corp draws isn’t great. Neither is the dynamic of “sorry, but I need to take 3-5 minutes to figure out if I can combo”; trying to figure out combo lines with a ticking round timer and/or the pressure of the cut was an extremely stressful experience!

-

Finally: hell yeah, Snarebears! This deck is nasty, and it belongs to the team more than it belongs to me.

decks.description_html:
👺

This deck serves as a baseline example of how I play Esa. This is the set of cards i usually prefer, with sometimes some minor tweaks based on how I feel. There's a lot of spices you can include/slots you can tweak which i will expand on down below, but is there is certainly directions unexplored this deck hasn't been taken in, so feel free to experiment.

The history

Back when I was preparing for my very first tournament about 1,5 years ago i really didnt know what runner to play, everything i tried felt awkward and unnatural. When discussing this with my local ~~testing partner~~ jank master Lyon at the time, he suggested Esa(he regrets it ever since) as I played it vs him once and it seemed to be my style. Having totally forgotten that at the time i took this deck by NNJ for a spin, whose roots date back to this deck by tuno i think. It went so well that i ended up finishing second! In the stack of alt arts I was generously offered to pick from by Veronica was:

This beautiful papercraft esa by nin419 I play to this day, both on jnet and irl. I've not looked at another runner since (except that one time i went to worlds and decided to play hosh and it went really bad and i will never betray xem again i promise).

Why play esa

nuff said

The deck

45 cards. Sleak, streamlined and fast. This deck is like an electric car in a field of diesel trucks. We go fast, get in, get out. Win or lose(but usually winning). I wil try to give some pointers on how to play the deck later, let's go over the moving parts first.

The engine

3x Ghosttongue

3x Nuka

This is the foundation of the deck. Without this, we won't be going anywhere fast.

The backup engine

3x Fermenter

1x Nurse Hạnh

These cards are meant to fill the 'dead air' for when our engine isn't totally running yet or when there's hiccups along the way. Kinda like our veggies.

The electricity

3x Steelskin Scarring

3x Strike Fund

2x Creative Commission

3x Raindrops Cut Stone

3x Sure Gamble

2-3x Running Hot

0-2x Wildcat Strike

0-2x The Price

Because our engine makes very efficient use of its fuel, we can churn through a lot of these in a short amount of time with huge efficiency rates. This means that we can stay on our feet(or wheels.. why did i do this metaphore to myself) during a game and dip low to keep up the pressure after which we bounce back with ease. Because our engine won't always be running in every game the density of these is very high meaning that we still have some money if we don't draw our ghosttongue early enough.

Some slots here are flexible:

  • Running Hot

I know, it's the best card in our deck. Why the hell would we want to play only 2 of it. I've said this myself before too, and sometimes I am mad at myself for only playing two. The thing is, it's not great in your opening hand and we don't end up playing all three copies in almost all of our games. Plus we can use katorga for one in a pinch. The main reason it's 2 is measured response, the bane of our existence. Feel free to play 3 though as its rad and fun and so sick to have more turns than your opponent.

  • Wildcat Strike

I have a love hate relationship with this card, sometimes it's really good. Sometimes you draw it when you're already down and you want to rip it apart. It's also dead near the end of your deck.

  • The price

This seems silly in a deck with 26 events and 19 installables right. Well it is! But surprisingly it's still quite good. The deck has a much harder time keeping up when we dont find our engine pieces or parts of the The spiked metal bumper with a cyclops and a wet cat with a gun attached to it™. The price always puts us closer to these cards when played, even if it whiffs. It has a nice side-benefit of being able to tutor from with Katorga.

The spiked metal bumper with a cyclops and a wet cat with a gun attached to it™

3x Botulus

1x Begemot

1x Rising Tide

1x Revolver

1x Abaasy

This is how we ram our face into things 😉. So in the past esa didnt have to use all of these actual breakers, having access to bankhar and/or laamb/dolls to cheat through non-barriers. Unfortunately in current day these tools are not available to us anymore, so we have to lean heavily on revolver and botulus. In some metas, especially when jinteki glacier is popular it would be wise to run two guns. In all other cases the regulated mandatory face™ will suffice for dealing with ice. I usually get a lot of questions about the breakers so i will go through them one-by-one:

  • Botulus

Our main long-term ice solution. I usually mainly target these at centrals, hq --> rd --> archives in order of importance (results may vary based on matchup, rd and archives can often be interchanged). I also try to prioritize getting the ice to be rezzed before plopping a botulus on it, but thats not always realistic.

  • Begemot

The cat, who doesn't love this guy. Hes so goofy. Very big tho. Hard to install sometimes. Dont wanna install it just to break Tatu-Bolas or Pings. Eats dolphins and bird summoner for lunch though.

  • Rising Tide

Tiny wave nobody really cares about. Much happier to instal it just to break Tatu-Bolas or Pings. Hates dolphins and bird summoner. btw check out this sick dutch-exclusive alt by Brindelmold Juno commissioned:

Come pay us a visit!

  • Revolver

Gun go pew pew. Really good. Makes facechecking a breeze. Dont be afraid to run out of bullets it rarely ever happens. Just put a botulus on it or whatever.

  • Abaasy

Aka abussy. Hate it forever. It's all we have though. Aint no way we're paying 4 to add a saw to our bumper™. We dont have that kinda money. No but really, 2 to install matters a lot here. Means that we can get it out of hand before taking damage in the matchups that we need a decoder. It's not meant to break big stuff multiple times but sometimes you have to. More often than not you can get by with pivoting to another server or plopping a botulus on it tho.

The fist-shape-tipped nuclear rocket launcher on the roof™

2x Chastushka

2x Finality

Just rip it dawg. Send it. No but really dont just send it i'm really sorry but we have to improve our reputation as esa players. We need to be better! We are not just a slot machine deck. It can be played this way but you will not consistently win games with this deck. Be agressive but also don't be aggressive if you know what i mean.

The airbags, roll cage and backup fist-shape tipped rocket launcher™

2x Marrow

2x Katorga Breakout

These are our mandatory safety measures. 2x marrow might seem odd, but we're just playing 2x our console like everyone else. Crim also has a bad time if they don't find Hermes early enough, and we can play pretty comfortably on 3-4 handsize if needed. Just try not to turn on threat 3-4 when you do.

I'll talk a bit more about katorga as well since i frequently get asked what to fetch with it, it'll be in order of most common to least common:

  1. Parts of The fist-shape-tipped nuclear rocket launcher on the roof™. The main purpose of these is to have your wincons when needed at all times. A common way to close the game is katorga archives fetching finality popping spin shuffling agendas back in the deck into finality.

  2. Dr.Nuka. This deck relies heavily on chaining nukas to keep it flowing, dont be afraid to spend a little tempo to fetch one on a drought.

  3. Running hot. Sometimes you just need more clicks in a turn.

  4. Steelskin. This is usually only into decks with a grinder gameplan but can be really clutch. A common line into au co is katorga archives fetching a steelskin for extra resilience on a big flip.

  5. Pinhole. It's a good card and sometimes you need more of it.

  6. Breaker of shame. So doing this means you fucked up lol. Happens to everyone but this is not the purpose of these. Happens to me too sometimes but it shouldn't come up often as the breaker suite is made to be cheap and playable before taking damage. Manage your risks!

The seatbelts

2x Pinhole Threading Everyone hates wearing these but we know we have to. Especially into a field with ob and auco.

The spices

So there are a couple of different blends that I have been testing this year. In the main deck posted above the speed stat is maxed out. Most of the suggestions below give up on a bit of that speed to solve certain problems.

Crewcharm

This was developed in a time where I ran into big ice often enough that I felt my ice solutions falling short. This is the build that gives up a significant amount of speed to achieve this however, really cutting into auco, funnty and other speedy matchups equity.

The Maemi package

The original face list had maemi in it and 2x bahia bands. Bahia bands is such a fun card. You can do a kickflip where you bahia archives, install a core damage card and flip access them at instant speed! Feels great. Unfortunately this is quite heavy on the slots causing the deck to go oversized. A solution to this can be cutting the creative commissions in favor of clean getaway and maybe a fermenter in favor of the maemi. The tricky part about making maemi value is ghosttongue makes all your 1 cost events not work with maemi bucks, so you need a good density of 2+ cost events that are easily playable. When this comes together it flows really good, but it's a good bit more bricky/draw order dependent which is why i don't prefer it.

Hippocampic Mechanocytes

The main reason to play this card is to be able to play running hot more times into decks with measured response as a wincon. Once this card is down it feels so cozy. Unfortunately it also has draw order issues and is a significant tempo hit to install, which is especially awkward into the tempo-oriented measured decks.

How to play

Here is where my writing skills kinda falter. I don't know how to describe this in a paragraph. There are so many specific things that can only be explained in the context of a game. I can give some bulletpoints for now:

  • Don't die. This should be your top priority. Don't flip archives if you can't survive double measured after. Don't contest the board if you can't eat an oppo. Don't facecheck hq if it can be winchester and lose you your spine. Play it safe. The win will come to you if you do.

  • Don't be afraid to lose your wincons. If you don't have the tempo to fist them, don't. The deck is made with so much redundancy that you can lose these to damage.

  • Manage your hand. Shrink down your hand by playing your nuka, breaker, nurse, econ operation or fementer first as much as possible when taking core damage to ensure the highest percentage of good stuff getting hit, usually this is a duplicate engine or safety piece, steelfund or one of your wincons. Nuka is there to draw back up after.

  • Don't overdraw too much. We all find ourselves in a situation sometimes where you really need that marrow or gun to be able to play the game. But usually it's not worth discarding half our deck for and then being gassed out for the rest of the game. Usually it's right to just click for credits and discard like 2 not very important cards and click nuka again at the start of your next turn. I know it feels bad but at least you're not making it worse.

  • Value your tempo over everything. As esa this involves sitting on your hands more often than not. I rarely ever play a chastushka on an open HQ early because it puts me in the hole more than it puts the corp.

  • Don't flip archives all the time. The win is never in there, trust me. Only do it to pressure spins or get nurse draw or on the final turn to win the game, otherwise it's just a waste of a click. More often than not you don't actually want to steal agendas in the early game because it turns on threat and causes you to have to play around measured when you're not ready for it yet.

  • Don't take more than one core damage in a turn. This is almost never worth it, but there are rare cases where it must be done(final turn running hot, etc).

  • Facecheck early and often. This deck needs to get its grubby little hands into everything the corp does to keep up the pressure. I facecheck an iced HQ turn one in almost every matchup.

  • Poke HQ. Don't let corps get away with hiding all of their agendies in there! Make sure to keep an eye out for windows of tempo to poke HQ in. I understand the desire for a card that tells you to go HQ/HQ multiaccess but the times you can get into HQ are so unpredictable and usually not very frequent that poking for singles is really the best way.
